questions.promptHtml:
A student carries a 12 kg suitcase 60 m along a level corridor at a constant speed, then lifts it 1.5 m onto a rack. Take g = 10 N/kg.

(a) Calculate the work done on the suitcase while carrying it along the corridor. (2)
(b) Calculate the work done lifting it onto the rack. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Zero 1

Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force. The supporting force is vertical while the motion is horizontal, so the distance in the direction of the force is zero 1

(b) The force needed equals the weight: W = m × g = 12 × 10 = 120 N 1

Work done = F × d = 120 × 1.5 1 = 180 J 1

Part (a) feels wrong because carrying a suitcase is tiring — but that energy goes into your muscles holding themselves tense, not into the suitcase. The physics definition is about the object.

Note that (b) is the same calculation as GPE = mgh: 12 × 10 × 1.5 = 180 J. Work done against gravity and gain in gravitational potential energy are the same quantity.

markScheme.point: (a) Zero
Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force. The supporting force is vertical while the motion is horizontal, so the distance in the direction of the force is zero
(b) The force needed equals the weight: W = m × g = 12 × 10 = 120 N
Work done = F × d = 120 × 1.5 = 180 J

modules.title: Motion in the Universe
modules.standfirst: Astrophysics: orbits, gravity, and the Doppler effect. Not on the September resit — the school's info pack lists six examinable topics and this is not one of them. It is on the full GCSE, so it lives here for next year.

intel.html:
Read this before you revise it. This topic is not on the September resit. The 136 examinable spec points in the school's info pack cover Forces and motion, Electricity, Waves, Energy, Solids/liquids/gases and Radioactivity — astrophysics is not among them, and the exam reference sheet notes that the orbital speed formula printed on the equation sheet is "for a topic not on this exam".

It is on the full Edexcel IGCSE, so it is here for Year 11. Leave it alone until the resit is done.

PaperWhat was asked
Topic test Q5 (7)Naming the universe, a galaxy and the solar system; fastest point in a comet's orbit; the force keeping it there; matching units of time to definitions
Topic test Q6 (5)ISS: orbital radius from speed and period, then the radius of the Earth
Topic test Q7 (10)Callisto: drawing an orbit, orbital speed to 3 s.f., gravitational field strength and weight on another world
Topic test Q8 (11)Satellite vs planet orbits; height of a geostationary orbit; the Doppler effect and why it does not apply to a geostationary satellite

Every numerical question in the school's topic test is the same equation rearranged — orbital speed — plus one weight calculation. Master that one formula and most of the marks follow.

subsections.html: Everything in orbit is falling. A satellite moves fast enough sideways that it keeps missing the thing it is falling towards, and gravity keeps bending its path into a circle. That single idea answers most of this topic.

subsections.heading: The scale: solar system, galaxy, universe
subsections.html:
Topic test Q5(a)

Three words in order of size, and the exam asks you to name them from a description:

  • Solar system — the Sun and everything orbiting it: planets, their moons, asteroids and comets.
  • Galaxy — a large collection of billions of stars (ours is the Milky Way).
  • Universe — space and all the galaxies in it.

subsections.heading: Gravity is the force, and only gravity
subsections.html:
Topic test Q5(b)(ii)

The force that keeps any object in orbit is gravity (the gravitational force or gravitational pull of the body it orbits). The mark scheme accepts those three, and rejects "gravitational potential" and "gravitational field strength" — those are related quantities, not the force itself.

Orbits are ellipses, not perfect circles. For a comet that means its distance from the Sun changes — and it moves fastest when it is closest to the Sun, slowest when it is furthest away. The topic test's multiple choice turned entirely on that: every wrong option was further from the Sun.

subsections.heading: Orbital speed — the one equation to memorise
subsections.html:
Topic test Q6, Q7(b), Q8(b)(i)

In one orbit an object travels the circumference of a circle, 2πr, in one time period T — so orbital speed v = 2πr ÷ T. (The equation and its symbol key are on the cheat sheet.)

Three rearrangements, all examined:

  • Find the speed (Callisto): convert the period to seconds first — 400 hours × 60 × 60 = 1 440 000 s — then v = 2π × 1 880 000 ÷ 1 440 000 = 8.20 km/s to 3 s.f.
  • Find the radius (ISS): r = vT ÷ 2π = 7.66 × (92.7 × 60) ÷ 2π = 6780 km.
  • Find the height above the surface: height = orbital radius − radius of the planet. The ISS orbits 409 km up, so the Earth's radius is 6780 − 409 = 6370 km. A geostationary satellite: r = 42 628 km, so height = 42 628 − 6400 = 36 000 km.

Two marks die here every time. Convert the period to seconds before substituting (24 hours = 86 400 s), and remember the orbital radius is measured from the centre of the planet — so the height above the surface is always the radius minus the planet's radius. The topic test asked for the difference explicitly in three separate questions.

subsections.heading: Gravitational field strength and weight elsewhere
subsections.html:
Topic test Q7(c)

g is the gravitational field strength in N/kg — the pull on each kilogram. On Earth it is about 10 N/kg; on Callisto 1.2; on our Moon 1.6.

Weight follows the same equation everywhere: W = m × g — mass never changes, but g does. (On the cheat sheet.)

To move a weight between two worlds, find the mass first: an object weighing 59 N on the Moon has mass 59 ÷ 1.6 = 37 kg, so on Callisto it weighs 37 × 1.2 = 44 N.

Why does Callisto pull less than our Moon despite being more massive? Because field strength depends on mass and radius — Callisto has a larger radius (it is less dense), so its surface sits further from its centre and the pull there is weaker. Any one of "larger radius", "lower density" or "smaller core" scored the mark.

subsections.heading: Satellites: what orbits what
subsections.html:
Topic test Q8(a)

The comparison question wants both halves stated: a satellite orbits a planet whereas a planet orbits a star; or the planet's orbital radius and period are greater. For the similarity: both orbit something, and both have the same shape of orbit (circular or elliptical).

A geostationary satellite has a period of exactly 24 hours, so it stays above the same point on the equator — which is why a satellite dish can be bolted in place.

subsections.heading: The Doppler effect
subsections.html:
Spec 3.8 — this part IS examinable · Topic test Q8(b)(ii)–(iii)

When a source of waves moves relative to an observer, the observed wavelength and frequency change. The three-mark explanation:

The script

1. The speed of the waves is constant 1

2. If the source moves away, the wavefronts spread out — the wavelength increases 1

3. Since speed = frequency × wavelength, a longer wavelength at constant speed means a lower observed frequency 1

And the trick question: why are the radio waves from a geostationary satellite not Doppler-shifted? Because there is no relative motion between the satellite and the point on the Earth's surface — the distance never changes — so there is no change in wavelength or frequency.

This is the one part of the module that is examinable on the resit, because Doppler sits in the Waves topic (spec 3.8) rather than in astrophysics.

The one equation everything follows from

v = 2πr ÷ T. Period in seconds, radius from the centre of the body. Height above the surface = orbital radius − planet radius.

Orbital speed — memorisev = (2 × π × r) ÷ Tv = orbital speed · r = orbital radius from the centre · T = time period of one orbit, in seconds
Weight — memoriseW = m × gW = weight (N) · m = mass (kg) · g = gravitational field strength (N/kg) — mass is constant, weight is not

questions.promptHtml: A satellite is in a stable orbit and its engines are off. Nothing is pushing it forwards — so why doesn't it slow down and fall?
questions.answerHtml:
Nothing needs to push it forwards, because in space there is essentially no air resistance — no friction to slow it down. Newton's first law does the rest: with no force along its direction of travel, its speed stays constant.

Gravity is acting, but it pulls at right angles to the motion — towards the centre of the Earth. That force doesn't speed the satellite up or slow it down; it continuously changes the direction of the velocity, bending the straight-line path into a circle.

So the satellite genuinely is falling towards Earth the whole time — it is just moving sideways fast enough that the Earth's surface curves away beneath it at the same rate.

questions.promptHtml: The ISS orbits at 409 km with speed 7.66 km/s and period 92.7 minutes. Work out the Earth's radius — and explain why the answer is not 409 km short of something.
questions.answerHtml:
Step 1 — period in seconds: 92.7 × 60 = 5562 s.

Step 2 — rearrange v = 2πr/T: r = vT ÷ 2π = 7.66 × 5562 ÷ 6.283 = 6780 km (3 s.f.).

Step 3: that 6780 km is measured from the centre of the Earth, because that is where the orbit is centred. The station is 409 km above the surface, so the surface sits at 6780 − 409 = 6370 km from the centre — which is the Earth's radius, and matches the real value of about 6371 km.

The reason it isn't "409 km short of something" is that the formula never knew about the surface at all — 2πr is the circumference of the circle the station actually travels, and that circle is centred on the Earth's core.

questions.promptHtml: Callisto is more massive than our Moon, yet its surface gravity is weaker (1.2 N/kg versus 1.6). How can more mass produce less pull?
questions.answerHtml:
Because surface gravity depends on two things: how much mass is pulling, and how far you are from the centre of it.

Callisto is considerably bigger across, so standing on its surface puts you much further from its centre than standing on the Moon does. That extra distance weakens the pull more than the extra mass strengthens it, and the net result is a lower g.

Any one of these scored the mark: Callisto has a larger radius, a lower density, or a smaller core. What does not score is anything about its distance from the Sun or its orbital radius — those are irrelevant to surface gravity.

questions.promptHtml: A satellite broadcasts radio waves at a fixed frequency. Explain why a geostationary satellite's signal shows no Doppler shift, while a low-orbit satellite passing overhead does.
questions.answerHtml:
The Doppler effect needs relative motion between source and observer — specifically, the distance between them must be changing.

Geostationary: its period is 24 hours, exactly matching the Earth's rotation, so it hovers above the same point. The distance to your dish never changes, so the wavefronts arrive at exactly the rate they left. No wavelength change, no frequency change.

Low orbit: it sweeps across the sky in minutes. As it approaches, the wavefronts bunch up — shorter wavelength, higher observed frequency. As it recedes, they spread out — longer wavelength, lower frequency. The signal's frequency appears to slide downwards as it passes overhead.

Throughout, the waves themselves travel at the speed of light. It is the wavelength that changes, and frequency follows because v = fλ with v fixed.

questions.promptHtml: Two satellites orbit Earth, one twice as far out as the other. Using v = 2πr/T alone, can you say which travels faster? What does the real answer depend on?
questions.answerHtml:
From that equation alone, no. It links three quantities: double r, and the speed doubles only if T stays the same. But T does not stay the same — a satellite further out takes longer to go round, and the formula does not tell you by how much.

In reality the further satellite moves more slowly: gravity is weaker further out, so less speed is needed to stay in orbit. The ISS at 409 km does 7.66 km/s and laps the Earth in 93 minutes; a geostationary satellite 36 000 km up manages only 3.1 km/s and takes a full day.

For the exam, the safe version is the comet fact: within one elliptical orbit, an object moves fastest when closest and slowest when furthest away.

modules.title: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
modules.standfirst: Magnets, the fields that currents make, the force that drives motors and loudspeakers, and the induced voltage that makes generators and transformers work. It came up in every one of the ten real papers. This is a Year 11 topic, taught in Year 11 for the GCSE in summer 2027. Electromagnets, field patterns for coils, the force on a moving charge and everything about transformers are Physics-only (P).

intel.html:
Every one of the ten real Edexcel papers from 2022 to 2024 has a question on this topic. Most are short 7–10 mark questions: a field pattern, a practical, a "describe the construction", then a short calculation or explanation.

PaperWhat was asked
2024 Edexcel 1P Q6 (8)Arrows on the field lines near a south pole, which material is magnetic (nickel), how field lines show field strength, why iron is attracted and why it is not a permanent magnet
2024 Edexcel 2P Q6 (7)Construction of an electromagnet; left-hand rule for a proton in a magnetic field, and why its velocity changes
2023 Edexcel 1P Q12 (10)Metal detector: why a coil has a field, d.c. versus a.c., why a current is induced in a gold ring, how a loudspeaker makes sound

2023 Edexcel 2P Q6 (9)National Grid: why a step-up transformer is used, the turns-ratio formula and a calculation, why a transformer will not work on d.c.
2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q2 (7)Uniform field between two magnets, why steel is used for magnets, why a voltage is induced in a moving wire and how to increase it
2023 Edexcel Jan 2P Q6 (8)Field around a straight wire through a card, how to show it, why two wires carrying current attract
2022 Edexcel 1P Q12(a)–(c) (4)Induced current as a wire moves between magnet poles: poles reversed, wire moved faster, a more sensitive meter
2022 Edexcel 2P Q3(a) (5)Phone charger: output power from P = I × V, then the input current for a 100% efficient transformer
2022 Edexcel 2P Q3(c) (4)Explain how a step-down transformer works

2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q4 (9)Planning an investigation into the field strength at different distances from a solenoid, then testing a suggested relationship
2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q6(a) (4)MRI scanner: describe the construction of an electromagnet
2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q6(b)(iv)–(v) (3)Evidence from an oscilloscope trace that a current is a.c.; the a.c. supply symbol

Three patterns stand out. "Describe the construction of an electromagnet" came up twice for 3 or 4 marks. The field-plotting practical (compass or iron filings) came up twice. And induction answers need the words "cuts the field lines" or "changing magnetic field", every time.

On the electromagnet question (2024 2P Q6(a)) the mark scheme says "reject explicit reference to bar magnet". An electromagnet has no permanent magnet in it. It is a coil, a current and a soft iron core.

On the motor question (2022 Jan 1P Q12(b)(i)): "ignore references to attraction / repulsion". The marks are for the fields interacting and the forces on the two sides of the coil, not for poles pulling on poles.

subsections.html: The whole topic hangs on three ideas. A current makes a magnetic field. A current in a magnetic field feels a force. A changing magnetic field induces a voltage. Motors and loudspeakers use the second; generators and transformers use the third. The units you need are the ampere (A), the volt (V) and the watt (W) (spec 6.1).

subsections.heading: Magnets, magnetic materials and induced magnetism
subsections.html:
Spec 6.2, 6.3, 6.5 · 2024 Edexcel 1P Q6(b), (d) · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q2(b) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1P Q1(b)(i), (c)

Like poles repel, unlike poles attract, and a magnet attracts magnetic materials, which are only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Copper, aluminium, zinc, plastic and wood are not magnetic. In 2024 the answer was nickel; copper, plastic and zinc were the wrong options.

When a piece of iron is placed in a magnetic field, it becomes a magnet itself. This is induced magnetism. The chain for "why is the iron attracted":

  1. The iron is in the magnet's field, so magnetism is induced in it.
  2. The end of the iron nearest the magnet becomes the opposite pole (next to a south pole it becomes a north pole).
  3. Opposite poles attract, so the iron is pulled towards the magnet.

This is why a magnetic material is attracted to either pole, and never repelled. Only a magnet can be repelled by a magnet.

Hard and soft magnetic materials behave differently when the field is removed:

MaterialBehaviourUsed for
Magnetically hard (steel)Hard to magnetise, but keeps its magnetism; hard to demagnetisePermanent magnets
Magnetically soft (iron)Easily magnetised and loses its magnetism easily when the field is removedElectromagnet cores, transformer cores

✗ "Iron is a soft magnet." ✓ "Iron is a soft magnetic material; it loses its magnetism when it is removed from the field." In 2024 the scheme said "ignore iron is a soft magnet" and "ignore iron is a temporary magnet".

✗ "The iron is charged." Magnetism is not charge. The 2024 scheme: "ignore references to charge".

subsections.html:
Spec 6.4, 6.6, 6.7 · 2024 Edexcel 1P Q6(a), (c) · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q2(a), (c) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1P Q1(a), (b)(ii), (d)

A magnetic field line shows the direction of the force on a north pole placed at that point, so field lines go from north to south outside a magnet. Where the lines are closer together the field is stronger; further apart means weaker. Field lines never cross.

2024 asked for arrows on the lines near a south pole: they point towards the south pole. Any arrow pointing away from it was rejected.

Practical: plotting the field of a bar magnet

Compass method (3 marks): put the magnet on paper. Place a plotting compass near one pole and mark the direction its needle points with a dot. Move the compass so its tail is on the dot and mark again. Repeat, then join the dots to make a field line. Start from different points to draw more lines.

Iron filings method (3 marks): put a sheet of paper or card over the magnet, sprinkle iron filings thinly on it, then tap the card gently so the filings line up along the field lines.

Filings show the shape but not the direction. Only a compass shows the direction.

For two bar magnets, do the same with the magnets placed end to end. Between opposite poles the lines join across the gap; between like poles they push apart, leaving a neutral point in the middle where the field is zero.

A uniform field is the same strength and direction everywhere. To make one, place two magnets with opposite poles (N facing S) close together and parallel. Between them the field lines are:

  1. straight
  2. parallel
  3. evenly spaced

Any two of those three words earned the 2 marks in 2023 Jan 1P Q2(c).

✗ "The field gets weaker because the force is smaller." ✓ "The field lines get further apart, which shows a weaker field." 2024's scheme said "ignore references to forces" here: the answer is about the spacing of the lines.

subsections.heading: The magnetic field around a current
subsections.html:
Spec 6.8, 6.10P · 2023 Edexcel Jan 2P Q6(a) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q4

A current in a wire produces a magnetic field around it. Switch the current off and the field disappears. Reverse the current and the field reverses. The field patterns (Physics only, 6.10P):

ShapeField pattern
Straight wireConcentric circles centred on the wire, in a plane at right angles to it. The circles get further apart further from the wire, because the field is weaker there.
Flat circular coilCircles around each side of the coil, which bend together so the lines through the centre of the coil are nearly straight.
Solenoid (a long coil)Like a bar magnet outside. Inside, the lines are straight, parallel and evenly spaced: a strong, uniform field.

For the direction around a straight wire, use the right-hand grip rule: point your right thumb along the current, and your fingers curl the way the field goes. So a current going down through a card, seen from above, gives a clockwise field. That was the direction arrow the 2023 Jan scheme wanted.

2023 Jan 2P Q6(a)(i): the 3-mark drawing

One circle centred on the wire, in the plane of the card · at least two concentric circles · a direction arrow (clockwise for current going down). To show the pattern, use iron filings and tap the card, or several plotting compasses around the wire.

subsections.heading: Electromagnets
subsections.html:
Spec 6.9P · 2024 Edexcel 2P Q6(a) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q6(a)

An electromagnet is a coil of wire (a solenoid) wrapped around a soft iron core, with a current in the coil. The four things the mark schemes look for:

  1. a coil of insulated wire (or a solenoid)
  2. a current in the coil, from a cell, battery or power supply
  3. a core inside the coil
  4. made of a named magnetic material: (soft) iron

The iron core makes the field much stronger. It must be soft iron so that the electromagnet loses its magnetism when the current is switched off. That on/off control is the whole point of an electromagnet: scrapyard cranes, relays, door locks and MRI scanners.

To make an electromagnet stronger: increase the current, add more turns to the coil, or use an iron core (if it has none).

2024 2P Q6(a) scheme: "ignore steel", "reject indication of a complete (iron) loop" and "reject explicit reference to bar magnet".

✗ "A bar magnet with wire round it." ✗ "A steel core." ✓ "A coil of wire wrapped around a soft iron core, with a current in the coil."

subsections.heading: The motor effect and the left-hand rule
subsections.html:
Spec 6.12, 6.13, 6.14 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 2P Q6(b) · 2024 Edexcel 2P Q6(b)(i)

A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force, because the field made by the current interacts with the magnet's field. This is the motor effect. The chain:

  1. The current in the wire produces its own magnetic field around the wire.
  2. This field interacts with the field of the magnet.
  3. The result is a force on the wire.

The force is biggest when the wire is at right angles to the field. If the wire is parallel to the field there is no force.

Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction. Hold the thumb and first two fingers of your left hand at right angles to each other:

  1. First finger = Field (north to south)
  2. seCond finger = Current (positive to negative)
  3. thuMb = Motion (the direction of the force)

What changes the force (6.14):

ChangeEffect on the force
Bigger currentBigger force
Stronger magnetic fieldBigger force
Reverse the currentForce reverses direction
Reverse the field (swap the poles)Force reverses direction
Reverse bothForce is in the same direction as before

Two parallel wires carrying current in the same direction attract. Each wire sits in the field of the other, so each has a current in a magnetic field and feels a force. The forces are equal in size and opposite in direction (2023 Jan 2P Q6(b)).

✗ "The wires attract because they have opposite charges." The 2023 Jan scheme: "reject reference to opposite charge". It is a magnetic force between currents, not an electrostatic one.

✗ Using the right hand. The left hand is for the force on a current (motors). The right hand only gives the direction of the field around a wire.

subsections.heading: The force on a moving charged particle
subsections.html:
Spec 6.11P · 2024 Edexcel 2P Q6(b)

A charged particle moving through a magnetic field feels a force, as long as it is not moving parallel to the field. A current is just moving charge, so this is the same motor effect.

Use the left-hand rule with the second finger along the current:

  1. For a positive particle (a proton), the current is in the direction it moves.
  2. For a negative particle (an electron), the current is opposite to the direction it moves.

The force is always at right angles to the velocity. So it changes the particle's direction but not its speed, and the particle curves round in an arc. As the direction changes, the direction of the force changes too, but its size stays the same.

2024 2P Q6(b)(iii) asked why the proton's velocity changes. The answer is that its direction changes. The scheme said "ignore idea of speed or magnitude of velocity changes". The speed does not change.

subsections.heading: Using the motor effect: d.c. motors and loudspeakers
subsections.html:
Spec 6.12 · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1P Q12(b) · 2023 Edexcel 1P Q12(c)

In a motor, the forces on the two sides of a coil are in opposite directions, so the coil turns.

  1. There is a current in the coil, so the coil has a magnetic field.
  2. This field interacts with the field of the permanent magnet.
  3. This produces a force on each side of the coil.
  4. The current goes one way along one side and back along the other, so the forces on opposite sides are in opposite directions. One side is pushed up, the other down, and the coil rotates.

A split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn, so the forces keep turning the coil the same way. To make the motor faster: bigger current, stronger magnet, more turns on the coil. To reverse it: reverse the current or swap the poles.

A loudspeaker uses the same effect with alternating current:

  1. An alternating current passes through a coil attached to the cone.
  2. The coil's field interacts with the field of a permanent magnet, causing a force on the coil.
  3. The a.c. keeps changing direction, so the force keeps changing direction.
  4. The coil and cone are pushed back and forth: they vibrate, making sound waves in the air.

2022 Jan 1P Q12(b)(i) scheme: "ignore references to attraction / repulsion". ✗ "The north pole of the coil is attracted to the south pole of the magnet." ✓ "The fields interact, producing a force; the forces on opposite sides of the coil are in opposite directions."

2023 1P Q12(c) scheme on the loudspeaker: "ignore fields cutting". Cutting field lines is induction, a different effect. A loudspeaker is the motor effect.

subsections.heading: Electromagnetic induction
subsections.html:
Spec 6.15 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q2(d) · 2022 Edexcel 1P Q12(a)–(c) · 2023 Edexcel 1P Q12(b)(ii)

A voltage is induced in a conductor when it moves through a magnetic field and cuts the field lines, or when the magnetic field through a coil changes. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, the induced voltage drives an induced current.

No movement and no change means no induced voltage. A wire held still between two magnets gives a zero reading. A wire moved along the field lines (not cutting them) also gives zero.

To increase the induced voltage:

  1. move the wire (or magnet) faster
  2. use a stronger magnet (or move the magnets closer together)
  3. turn the wire into a coil, or use more turns on the coil

To reverse it: move the wire the other way, or reverse the poles. 2022 1P Q12 showed a reading of 2.8 mA; with the poles reversed the answer was −2.8 mA (same size, opposite direction); moving faster gave a bigger reading.

The metal detector in 2023 1P Q12 used a changing field instead of movement: the a.c. in the transmitter coil makes a changing magnetic field; this field cuts the gold ring; an alternating voltage is induced in the ring.

2023 Jan 1P Q2(d)(i) scheme: "ignore wire interacting with field lines". ✗ "The wire interacts with the field." ✓ "The wire cuts the magnetic field lines."

Part (d)(ii) also said "ignore "bigger" magnets". A bigger magnet is not necessarily a stronger one. Say stronger.

subsections.heading: Generators
subsections.html:
Spec 6.16

A generator makes electricity by rotating a magnet inside a coil, or rotating a coil inside a magnetic field, so that the coil keeps cutting field lines and a voltage is induced.

TypeWhat turnsExample
Rotating magnetA magnet spins inside a fixed coil, so the field through the coil keeps changingA bicycle dynamo
Rotating coilA coil spins between the poles of a magnet, so its sides cut the field linesA simple a.c. generator

Each side of the coil moves up through the field, then down through it, so the induced voltage keeps reversing. The output is alternating.

The size of the induced voltage increases if you:

  1. rotate the coil or magnet faster
  2. use a stronger magnet
  3. use more turns on the coil

Rotating faster also makes the a.c. change direction more often, so the frequency goes up too.

subsections.heading: Transformers and the two transformer equations
subsections.html:
Spec 6.17P, 6.19P, 6.20P · 2022 Edexcel 2P Q3(a), (c) · 2023 Edexcel 2P Q6(a)(ii)–(iii), (b)

A transformer is two coils of wire, the primary and the secondary, wound on the same soft iron core. It changes the size of an alternating voltage.

How it works, the 4-mark chain from 2022 2P Q3(c):

  1. An alternating current in the primary coil produces a magnetic field.
  2. Because the current keeps changing, this is a changing magnetic field in the iron core.
  3. The core carries the changing field to the secondary coil, where the field lines cut the coil.
  4. This induces an alternating voltage in the secondary coil.

Step-up transformer: more turns on the secondary, so the output voltage is bigger. Step-down: fewer turns on the secondary, so the output voltage is smaller.

input voltage ÷ output voltage = primary turns ÷ secondary turns
both voltages in the same unit · the turns are just numbers

input power = output power: primary voltage × primary current = secondary voltage × secondary current
for a 100% efficient transformer · voltages in V · currents in A

2023 2P Q6(a)(iii): the 3-mark calculation

Input 15 kV, output 340 kV, 1400 turns on the primary. Find the secondary turns.

Substitution: 15 ÷ 340 = 1400 ÷ ns · rearrangement: ns = 1400 × 340 ÷ 15 · evaluation: ns = 31 733, about 32 000 turns.

The kV cancel out, so there is no need to convert to volts, as long as both voltages are in the same unit.

The power equation follows because a 100% efficient transformer wastes no energy: input power = output power. So if the voltage is stepped up, the current is stepped down by the same factor. 2022's phone charger: output 5.0 V × 1.2 A = 6.0 W, so input current = 6.0 ÷ 230 = 0.026 A.

2023 2P Q6(b): a transformer will not work on constant d.c. A constant current gives a constant magnetic field; induction needs a changing field; so no voltage is induced in the secondary.

When stating the formula (2023 2P Q6(a)(ii)) the scheme said "reject phrase `turns ratio'". Write the full equation, input voltage ÷ output voltage = primary turns ÷ secondary turns, not "voltage ratio = turns ratio".

subsections.heading: Transformers in the National Grid
subsections.html:
Spec 6.18P · 2023 Edexcel 2P Q6(a)(i)

Electricity is sent across the country at a very high voltage so that the current in the cables is small, which means less heating and less energy wasted.

power = current × voltage
power in watts (W) · current in amperes (A) · voltage in volts (V)

  1. At the power station, a step-up transformer increases the voltage to hundreds of thousands of volts.
  2. For the same power, P = I × V, a higher voltage means a lower current.
  3. A lower current means less heating in the cables, so less energy is wasted and thinner cables can be used.
  4. Near homes, step-down transformers reduce the voltage to a safe level, 230 V in the UK.

✗ "A high voltage wastes less energy." That skips the key step. ✓ "Stepping up the voltage reduces the current; a smaller current means less heating in the wires." Those are the two marks in 2023 2P Q6(a)(i). The scheme also said "ignore unqualified reference to efficiency".

subsections.heading: Mains a.c. and battery d.c.
subsections.html:
Spec 2.6 · 2023 Edexcel 1P Q12(b)(i) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q6(b)(iv)–(v)

Direct current (d.c.) flows in one direction only; alternating current (a.c.) continuously changes direction. A cell or battery supplies d.c. Mains electricity is a.c.

d.c.a.c.
SourceCell or batteryMains supply, generators
Direction of currentOne direction onlyKeeps reversing
Oscilloscope traceA flat horizontal lineA wave that goes above and below zero, again and again

2022 Jan 2P Q6(b)(iv) asked for the evidence on a trace that a current is a.c.: the trace goes both positive and negative, and it does so continuously. The a.c. supply symbol is a circle with two terminals and a sine wave inside.

✗ "a.c. goes back and forth once." ✓ "a.c. continuously changes direction." The 2023 scheme allowed "keeps changing direction, changes direction constantly". The word showing it repeats is what earns the mark.

subsections.heading: Protecting the user: insulation, earthing, fuses and circuit breakers
subsections.html:
Spec 2.2 · 2023 Edexcel 1P Q3(b)

Each safety feature either stops you touching a live part, or cuts off the current when it gets too big.

FeatureHow it protects
InsulationPlastic or rubber around the wires. Plastic is an electrical insulator, so you cannot touch the live metal.
Double insulationThe whole outer case is made of plastic (an insulator), so even if a wire comes loose the case cannot become live. No earth wire is needed.
EarthingA metal case is connected to the earth wire. If the live wire touches the case, a large current flows to earth through the low-resistance earth wire, which blows the fuse. The case does not stay live.
FuseA thin wire in the live wire. If the current is bigger than the fuse rating, the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit, isolating the appliance and stopping the cable overheating.
Circuit breakerAn automatic switch that opens when the current is too large. It acts faster than a fuse and can be reset rather than replaced.

2023 1P Q3(b): the fuse questions

(i) How a fuse protects (3): the current exceeds the fuse rating · the fuse wire melts · the circuit is broken so the device is isolated.

(ii) Why 13 A is wrong for a TV drawing 0.31 A (2): the rating is much higher than the normal current · so a fault current could flow without the fuse melting, and the lead or TV could overheat or catch fire.

Choosing the right fuse from P = I × V is in Module 3: pick the rating just above the normal current.

2023 1P Q3(b)(i) scheme: "ignore fuse burns" and "ignore current increasing". ✗ "The fuse burns when the current increases." ✓ "When the current exceeds the fuse rating, the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit."

The sentences behind most of the marks

Field lines: go from N to S; closer together means a stronger field.

Uniform field: opposite poles facing; lines straight, parallel, evenly spaced.

Induced magnetism: the near end of the iron becomes the opposite pole, and opposite poles attract.

Electromagnet: a coil with a current, wrapped round a soft iron core.

Motor effect: the field of the current interacts with the magnet's field, producing a force. No force if the wire is parallel to the field.

Induction: the conductor cuts the field lines, or the field through the coil changes, so a voltage is induced.

Transformer: a.c. in the primary makes a changing field in the core, which induces a voltage in the secondary. No change, no voltage: it will not work on d.c.

Grid: step up the voltage, so the current is lower, so there is less heating in the cables.

subsections.html:
All three are memorise equations: none is on the formula sheet.

Transformer turns ratio — memoriseVp ÷ Vs = np ÷ nsVp = primary (input) voltage (V) · Vs = secondary (output) voltage (V) · np = turns on the primary · ns = turns on the secondary
Transformer power, 100% efficient — memoriseVp × Ip = Vs × Isinput power = output power · Ip = primary current (A) · Is = secondary current (A)
Electrical power — memoriseP = I × VP = power (W) · I = current (A) · V = voltage (V)

questions.promptHtml: An unmagnetised iron nail is attracted to the north pole of a magnet, and also to the south pole. Why is it never repelled? And what is the only sure test that a piece of metal is a magnet?
questions.hint: Which pole is induced at the end nearest the magnet?
questions.answerHtml:
The nail becomes a magnet itself when it is in the field: magnetism is induced in it.

The end nearest the magnet always becomes the opposite pole. Next to a north pole it becomes a south pole; next to a south pole it becomes a north pole. Opposite poles attract, so the nail is attracted either way.

So attraction proves nothing: a magnet attracts both magnets and magnetic materials. Repulsion is the only sure test. Only two magnets can push each other away.

questions.promptHtml: Permanent magnets are made of steel. Electromagnet and transformer cores are made of soft iron. Why not the other way round?
questions.answerHtml:
A permanent magnet has to keep its magnetism. Steel is magnetically hard: once magnetised, it stays magnetised.

An electromagnet has to lose its magnetism when the current is switched off, or the crane could never drop the car. Soft iron does that.

A transformer core is even more demanding. The a.c. reverses many times a second, so the core has to be magnetised, demagnetised and remagnetised the other way, over and over. Soft iron follows those changes easily. A steel core would resist them.

questions.promptHtml: A wire carrying a current lies between two magnets. Turned one way it feels a strong force. Turned so it runs along the field lines, it feels no force at all. Why?
questions.answerHtml:
The force comes from charges moving across the field. A current is moving charge, and a charge moving through a magnetic field feels a force only if it is not moving parallel to the field (spec 6.11P).

At right angles, the charges cross the field lines as directly as possible, so the force is biggest. Along the field lines, the charges never cross them, so there is no force.

This is also why the left-hand rule only works with your fingers at right angles. The rule describes the case where the current is perpendicular to the field.

questions.promptHtml: Without a split-ring commutator, a motor coil turns about a quarter of a turn and then just rocks to a stop. Why? And how does the commutator fix it?
questions.answerHtml:
One side of the coil is pushed up and the other down. That turns the coil until it is upright. Past that point, the side that was pushed up is now on the other side of the axle. The same forces now turn the coil back. So it rocks and stops.

The commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn. Just as the sides swap places, the current in each side reverses, so the forces reverse too. The side on the left is always pushed up and the side on the right always pushed down, so the coil keeps turning the same way.

questions.promptHtml: A student connects a transformer to a battery. The secondary coil gives no output, even though there is a current in the primary and the core is magnetised. Explain.
questions.answerHtml:
The core is magnetised, so there is a magnetic field through the secondary coil. But induction does not need a field; it needs a changing field.

A battery gives a constant d.c. current, so the field in the core is constant. Nothing changes through the secondary coil, so no voltage is induced.

That is the whole reason mains electricity is a.c. and why transformers only work on a.c. (There is a brief flick of voltage at the instant the switch is closed, because the field changes as it builds up. Then nothing.)

questions.promptHtml: A power station sends out 100 MW. Compare the current in the cables at 25 kV and at 400 kV. Why does the difference matter?
questions.answerHtml:
From P = I × V, the current is I = P ÷ V.

At 25 kV: I = 100 000 000 ÷ 25 000 = 4000 A. At 400 kV: I = 100 000 000 ÷ 400 000 = 250 A. The current is 16 times smaller.

The heating in a cable depends on the current. A smaller current means much less heating, so much less energy is wasted heating the cables and the surroundings. That is why the step-up transformer is there.

The high voltage is dangerous, so step-down transformers bring it down to 230 V before it reaches homes.

questions.promptHtml: A step-up transformer turns 230 V into 4600 V. A student says "you get twenty times more out than you put in". What is wrong?
questions.answerHtml:
The voltage goes up twenty times, but the power does not. At best (100% efficient) input power = output power, so Vp × Ip = Vs × Is.

If the voltage goes up by 20 times, the current must go down by 20 times. With 2.0 A in the primary: 230 × 2.0 = 460 W in, so the secondary current is 460 ÷ 4600 = 0.10 A.

A transformer trades voltage for current. It can never give out more energy than it takes in; that would break conservation of energy.

questions.promptHtml: A metal kettle has an earth wire and a fuse. A plastic hairdryer has a fuse but no earth wire. Why does the kettle need both, and why is the hairdryer safe without an earth?
questions.answerHtml:
The kettle: if the live wire comes loose and touches the metal case, the case becomes live. Anyone touching it would get a shock.

The earth wire connects the case to earth through a very low resistance. So a large current flows straight to earth. That large current is more than the fuse rating, so the fuse melts and breaks the circuit. The earth wire and fuse work as a team: the earth wire makes the big current happen, and the fuse then cuts it off.

The hairdryer is double insulated. Its case is plastic, an insulator, so a loose live wire cannot make the case live. There is nothing for an earth wire to protect. It still has a fuse, to stop the cable overheating if too much current flows.

So as the proton's direction changes, the direction of the force changes too, while its size stays the same 1

drill.intro: Exam register now. Roughly one minute per mark. State formulas when asked, show substitutions, give units.

modules.title: Momentum
modules.standfirst: Momentum is mass × velocity, and in any collision or explosion the total momentum stays the same. The same idea explains why crumple zones, airbags, seat belts and helmets save lives. This is a Year 11 topic (taught in Year 11, for the GCSE in summer 2027), and every spec point in it is Physics-only.

intel.html:
Momentum came up in three of the ten real Edexcel papers, always on Paper 2P and always as a short, structured question near the start. The pattern is the same each time: a p = m × v calculation, then either conservation of momentum or force = change in momentum ÷ time, then a safety explanation.

PaperWhat was asked
2023 Edexcel 2P Q4 (7)Two birds, just before bird X catches bird Y: momentum of bird X, total momentum before, momentum after the catch, then the velocity of the two birds together
2022 Edexcel 2P Q2 (8)The unit of momentum (kg m/s); state the principle of conservation of momentum; two objects pushing apart from rest, find the velocity of one (−2.4 m/s); why an egg dropped on a carpet does not break
2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q1(b) (5)Airbags: state momentum = mass × velocity; momentum of a 72 kg driver at 13 m/s; force = change in momentum ÷ time (3200 N); how an airbag protects the driver

Two patterns are worth noticing. The equation p = m × v is asked for on its own, as a free mark. And every safety question is marked on the same three steps: longer time, smaller rate of change of momentum, smaller force.

On the egg and carpet in 2022, the mark scheme credited the "idea of carpet increases impact time" and then "carpet reduces rate of change of momentum". Both are needed. "The carpet is soft" scores nothing on its own.

On the airbag in January 2022, the scheme rejected one option because "increasing the force does not protect the driver". The airbag does not change how much momentum the driver loses. It changes how long that takes, and so makes the force smaller.

subsections.html: All of this module is Physics-only. It is small: one definition, one conservation law and one force equation, used in three kinds of question. The marks are lost on signs (momentum has a direction) and on vague wording in the safety explanations. Every heading below says where it was actually asked.

subsections.heading: Momentum = mass × velocity
subsections.html:
Spec 1.25P · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q1(b) · 2023 Edexcel 2P Q4(a)

Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity: the heavier and faster something is, the more momentum it has.

p = m × v
p = momentum in kg m/s · m = mass in kilograms (kg) · v = velocity in metres/second (m/s)

You must know this from memory. January 2022 gave a mark just for writing momentum = mass × velocity, and then a mark for 72 × 13 = 936 kg m/s. In 2023 the first bird had a mass of 0.41 kg and a speed of 13 m/s: 0.41 × 13 = 5.3 kg m/s.

A slow lorry can have more momentum than a fast bullet, because momentum depends on both mass and velocity. Neither one on its own tells you who has more.

✗ Using grams. A 58 g ball is 0.058 kg. Always convert to kilograms first.
✗ "momentum = mass × acceleration" — that is force.
✓ "momentum = mass × velocity", with the mass in kg and the velocity in m/s.

subsections.heading: The unit: kg m/s
subsections.html:
Spec 1.2P · 2022 Edexcel 2P Q2(a)

The unit of momentum is the kilogram metre per second, written kg m/s.

It comes straight from the equation: kilograms (mass) multiplied by metres per second (velocity). 2022 asked for it as a multiple-choice mark, and the wrong options were built from dividing by the mass, squaring the mass, or other wrong combinations. If you remember p = m × v, you can rebuild the unit every time.

The unit N s (newton second) is the same size of unit, because force × time = change in momentum. You will see it in some textbooks, but kg m/s is the unit this spec names, so use it.

✗ kg/m/s   ✗ kg m/s² (that is a newton)   ✗ kg² m/s
✓ kg m/s

subsections.heading: Momentum is a vector — choose a positive direction
subsections.html:
Spec 1.25P (with 1.13, 1.14) · 2022 Edexcel 2P Q2(b)(ii)

Momentum has a direction as well as a size, so before any calculation you choose one direction as positive and give everything moving the other way a minus sign.

Velocity is a vector, and mass is a scalar, so momentum is a vector. A 2 kg trolley moving right at 3 m/s has momentum +6 kg m/s. The same trolley moving left at 3 m/s has momentum −6 kg m/s. Two trolleys with those momenta have a total momentum of zero, not 12.

  1. Draw a quick arrow and write "right = +" (or whichever way you like).
  2. Write each velocity with its sign: things moving the other way are negative.
  3. Work out each momentum with its sign, then add them.
  4. If an answer comes out negative, it means "in the negative direction". Say which way that is.

In 2022, the answer to the push-apart question was −2.4 m/s. The minus sign simply meant it moved the opposite way to the other object. The mark scheme accepted it.

subsections.heading: Conservation of momentum
subsections.html:
Spec 1.27P · 2022 Edexcel 2P Q2(b)(i)

In a collision or explosion, the total momentum before is equal to the total momentum after, as long as no external forces act.

total momentum before = total momentum after

That sentence is the one-mark "state the principle" answer. The mark scheme's version also mentions "in the absence of external forces", so add it. External forces are things like friction or a push from outside; if they are small, you ignore them.

Why it is true: when two objects collide, by Newton's third law (module 01) they push on each other with equal and opposite forces, for exactly the same time. So one gains exactly the momentum the other loses. The total cannot change.

The method for every conservation question

1. Choose a positive direction.  ·  2. Total momentum before = add up m × v for everything, with signs.  ·  3. Write total momentum after in the same way, with the unknown as a letter.  ·  4. Set before = after and rearrange.

Write the equation out in full before you put numbers in. The mark schemes give a mark for "setting up equation using conservation of momentum", separate from the answer.

subsections.heading: Collisions where the objects join together
subsections.html:
Spec 1.27P · 2023 Edexcel 2P Q4 — 7 marks

When two objects stick together, they move off as one object with the combined mass, so the velocity after = total momentum ÷ total mass.

2023's question was two birds. Bird X (0.41 kg, 13 m/s) caught bird Y, flying the same way. The question took you through it one step at a time:

  1. Momentum of X = 0.41 × 13 = 5.33 kg m/s.
  2. Total momentum before = momentum of X + momentum of Y = 5.48 kg m/s.
  3. Total momentum after = the same, 5.48 kg m/s. That was a mark for knowing momentum is conserved.
  4. Total mass after = 0.58 kg, so velocity = 5.48 ÷ 0.58 = 9.4 m/s.

Notice the answer is between the two birds' starting speeds. The fast bird slows down; the slow bird speeds up. That is a quick check on any "join together" answer.

✗ Dividing the total momentum by the mass of one bird. After the catch they move together, so use the total mass.
✓ velocity after = total momentum ÷ (m₁ + m₂)

subsections.heading: Collisions where the objects bounce apart
subsections.html:
Spec 1.27P

If the objects move off separately, the total momentum after is the sum of two separate momenta, and it still equals the total before.

Example: a 0.16 kg snooker ball moving at 2.5 m/s hits a stationary 0.16 kg ball. The first ball carries on at 0.5 m/s. Find the second ball's velocity.

  1. Before: 0.16 × 2.5 + 0.16 × 0 = 0.40 kg m/s.
  2. After: 0.16 × 0.5 + 0.16 × v = 0.08 + 0.16v.
  3. 0.40 = 0.08 + 0.16v, so v = 0.32 ÷ 0.16 = 2.0 m/s.

If an object bounces back, its velocity after is negative. Forgetting that minus sign is the most common error in this whole topic.

subsections.heading: Explosions and recoil — starting from rest
subsections.html:
Spec 1.27P · 2022 Edexcel 2P Q2(b)(ii)

If everything starts at rest, the total momentum before is zero, so after the explosion the two parts have equal and opposite momentum.

"Explosion" means anything that pushes two objects apart from rest: a spring between two trolleys, two skaters pushing off each other, a gun firing a bullet, a person jumping off a boat.

2022's question had a 1.9 kg object moving off at 3.7 m/s and a 2.9 kg object. The mark scheme's working was:

0 = (1.9 × 3.7) + (2.9 × v)  →  v = −7.03 ÷ 2.9 = −2.4 m/s

The minus sign means the 2.9 kg object moves the opposite way. Note that the heavier object moves off more slowly. The two momenta are the same size (7.03 kg m/s each); the masses are not.

This is why a gun recoils. The bullet gets forward momentum, so the gun must get the same momentum backwards. The gun is much heavier, so its recoil speed is much smaller. (The pair of forces between bullet and gun is a Newton's third law pair, covered in module 01.)

subsections.heading: Force = change in momentum ÷ time
subsections.html:
Spec 1.28P · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q1(b)(iii)

A resultant force changes an object's momentum; the force equals the change in momentum divided by the time it takes.

F = (mv − mu) ÷ t
F = force (N) · m = mass (kg) · v = final velocity (m/s) · u = initial velocity (m/s) · t = time taken (s) · mv − mu = change in momentum (kg m/s)

This one is on the formula sheet, but you must know how to use it. In words: force = change in momentum ÷ time taken. So force is the rate of change of momentum.

January 2022: the driver's momentum of 936 kg m/s dropped to zero in 0.29 s. Force = 936 ÷ 0.29 = 3200 N (2 s.f.).

It is really F = m × a in disguise. (mv − mu) ÷ t = m × (v − u) ÷ t, and (v − u) ÷ t is the acceleration. Use whichever the question points you towards, but if it mentions momentum, use this one.

✗ Using the final momentum instead of the change. For something that stops, the change is all of its momentum; for something that speeds up from 10 m/s to 25 m/s, it is m × 25 − m × 10, not m × 25.
✓ Always work out mv − mu first, then divide by t.

subsections.heading: Change in momentum when something bounces
subsections.html:
Spec 1.28P, 1.25P

When an object bounces back, its momentum reverses, so the change in momentum is bigger than when it just stops.

A 0.20 kg ball hits a wall at 8.0 m/s and bounces back at 6.0 m/s. Take "towards the wall" as positive.

  1. mu = 0.20 × (+8.0) = +1.6 kg m/s.
  2. mv = 0.20 × (−6.0) = −1.2 kg m/s.
  3. mv − mu = −1.2 − 1.6 = −2.8 kg m/s. The size of the change is 2.8 kg m/s, away from the wall.

If the ball had simply stopped, the change would have been only 1.6 kg m/s. Bouncing needs a bigger change, so for the same contact time it needs a bigger force.

✗ 1.6 − 1.2 = 0.4 kg m/s. That treats both velocities as the same direction.
✓ −1.2 − (+1.6) = −2.8 kg m/s. The velocities are in opposite directions, so the sizes add.

subsections.heading: Momentum and safety: the argument
subsections.html:
Spec 1.26P · 2022 Edexcel 2P Q2(c) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q1(b)(iv)

In a crash your momentum has to fall to zero whatever happens; safety features make that take longer, so the rate of change of momentum, and so the force on you, is smaller.

Look at F = (mv − mu) ÷ t. In a crash, the change in momentum (mv − mu) is fixed: you go from your speed to zero. The only thing a safety feature can change is t. A bigger t on the bottom of the fraction means a smaller F.

The three-step script — one mark each

1. The feature increases the time taken for the person (or object) to stop.

2. The change in momentum is the same, so the rate of change of momentum is smaller.

3. So the force on the person is smaller, and there is less injury.

2022's egg on the carpet used exactly these steps: "idea of carpet increases impact time", then "carpet reduces rate of change of momentum", then a smaller force.

✗ "The airbag reduces the momentum." The driver's momentum still goes from the same value to zero, so the change is the same.
✗ "The airbag absorbs the force" or "cushions the impact". Too vague to score.
✓ "The airbag increases the time taken for the driver to stop, so the rate of change of momentum is smaller, so the force on the driver is smaller."

subsections.heading: Crumple zones, airbags, seat belts and helmets
subsections.html:
Spec 1.26P · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q1(b)

Each safety feature works the same way: it lets the stop happen over a longer time. Only the part that does the stretching or squashing changes.

FeatureWhat it doesWhy the force is smaller
Crumple zoneThe front and back of the car crumple (deform) in a crashThe car takes longer to stop, so the rate of change of momentum of the car and the people inside is smaller
AirbagInflates and then squashes as the driver moves into itThe driver's head and chest take longer to stop, so the force on them is smaller
Seat beltStretches slightly and holds the passenger in the seatThe passenger takes longer to stop, so the force is smaller; it also stops them hitting the windscreen
Cycle helmetA foam lining compresses when the head hits somethingThe head takes longer to stop, so the force on the skull is smaller

The same idea explains everyday things: catching a ball by pulling your hands back, bending your knees when you land from a jump, and soft playground surfaces. In each one, a longer stopping time means a smaller force.

subsections.heading: Choosing the right tool
subsections.html:
Spec 1.25P – 1.28P

Read what the question gives you and what it wants, then pick one of three tools.

The question mentionsUse
One object, its mass and velocityp = m × v
Two or more objects colliding, joining, or pushing apartConservation of momentum: total before = total after
A force, or a time for the collision (contact time, stopping time)F = (mv − mu) ÷ t
"Explain" how something makes a crash saferThe three-step script: longer time → smaller rate of change of momentum → smaller force

In the real papers these came in that order within one question. Part (a) was often p = m × v, and its answer fed into the next part. If you got part (a) wrong, the scheme usually still gave the later marks for using your own answer correctly, so always carry on.

The sentences behind most of the marks

Momentum = mass × velocity, in kg m/s. It is a vector: choose a positive direction and use minus signs.

Total momentum before = total momentum after, in any collision or explosion, as long as no external forces act.

Joined together: velocity after = total momentum ÷ total mass.

From rest: total momentum is zero, so the two parts move off with equal and opposite momentum.

Force = change in momentum ÷ time taken. Force is the rate of change of momentum.

Safety: increases the time to stop → smaller rate of change of momentum → smaller force.

questions.promptHtml: Why is momentum conserved in a collision? Explain it using forces, not just by stating the rule.
questions.hint: Newton's third law, and how long each force acts for.
questions.answerHtml:
When A hits B, A pushes on B and B pushes on A. By Newton's third law these forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.

They also act for exactly the same time, because they only exist while the two objects are touching.

Change in momentum = force × time. So B gains exactly as much momentum as A loses, in the same direction A was going. Add the two changes and you get zero.

The catch: this only works if nothing outside the two objects pushes on them. A big friction force from the ground is an external force, and then the total momentum of the two objects can change. That is why the rule says "in the absence of external forces".

questions.promptHtml: Which has more momentum: a 12 000 kg lorry rolling at 0.5 m/s, or a 0.01 kg bullet at 400 m/s?
questions.answerHtml:
Lorry: 12 000 × 0.5 = 6000 kg m/s. Bullet: 0.01 × 400 = 4 kg m/s.

The slow lorry has 1500 times the momentum of the fast bullet.

The point: momentum depends on mass and velocity together. "Fast" does not mean "lots of momentum", and nor does "heavy". You have to multiply. This is why a slowly rolling lorry is so hard to stop by hand.

questions.promptHtml: A rifle fires a bullet. The bullet and the rifle get momenta of exactly the same size. So why does the bullet fly off at hundreds of metres per second while the rifle only moves back slowly?
questions.answerHtml:
Before firing, everything is at rest, so the total momentum is zero. After firing, it must still be zero. So the bullet's forward momentum and the rifle's backward momentum are equal and opposite.

Momentum = mass × velocity. The same momentum shared by a small mass gives a large velocity; by a large mass, a small velocity.

A 4 kg rifle and a 0.01 kg bullet: the rifle is 400 times heavier, so it moves 400 times more slowly.

Same idea in 2022's push-apart question: the 2.9 kg object moved off more slowly (2.4 m/s) than the 1.9 kg one (3.7 m/s).

questions.promptHtml: A student says: "An airbag protects you because it reduces your momentum." What is wrong with this, and what should they say instead?
questions.hint: What is your momentum at the end of the crash, with or without the airbag?
questions.answerHtml:
With or without the airbag, you start at the car's speed and end at zero. So your change in momentum is the same either way. The airbag does not reduce it at all.

What changes is the time. Without an airbag, your head stops in a few milliseconds against the steering wheel. With one, it stops over a longer time as the bag squashes.

Force = change in momentum ÷ time. Same top, bigger bottom, so a smaller force.

The January 2022 mark scheme made the related point that increasing the force does not protect the driver: protection means a smaller force, and that comes from a longer time.

questions.promptHtml: A ball hits a wall and stops dead. An identical ball hits the wall at the same speed and bounces back at the same speed. The contact times are equal. Which ball feels the bigger force from the wall, and by how much?
questions.answerHtml:
Take towards the wall as positive, and call the momentum before +p.

Stops dead: momentum goes from +p to 0. Change = p.

Bounces back: momentum goes from +p to −p. Change = −p − p = 2p.

Same contact time, so the bouncing ball feels twice the force.

Why this matters: it is the reason signs matter so much. If you forget that the bounce-back velocity is negative, you calculate a change of zero, which is obviously wrong: the ball clearly was pushed.

questions.promptHtml: A cricketer catches a hard ball. Why does she pull her hands back as she catches it?
questions.answerHtml:
The ball's momentum has to fall to zero either way. The change in momentum is fixed.

By moving her hands back with the ball, she increases the time over which the ball stops.

So the rate of change of momentum is smaller, and the force on her hands is smaller. It stings less.

This is exactly the same argument as a crumple zone, an airbag, a seat belt or a helmet. Learn the argument once and it answers every version.

questions.promptHtml: Trolley A (2 kg) moves right at 3 m/s. Trolley B (2 kg) moves left at 3 m/s. They collide head-on and stick together. A student says the total momentum is 12 kg m/s, so they move off at 3 m/s. What should happen, and where did the student go wrong?
questions.answerHtml:
Take right as positive. A: 2 × (+3) = +6 kg m/s. B: 2 × (−3) = −6 kg m/s.

Total momentum = +6 + (−6) = 0. After sticking, the total is still 0, so they stop dead.

The student ignored direction and added the sizes. Momentum is a vector, so opposite directions cancel.

The habit that fixes it: write "right = +" at the start of every momentum question, before you write a single number.

questions.promptHtml: In the 2023 two-birds question, the momentum after the catch was the same as before, but the fast bird slowed down from 13 m/s. Where did its momentum go?
questions.answerHtml:
It was shared with the slower bird. After the catch, both birds move together at 9.4 m/s.

Bird X lost some momentum; bird Y gained exactly the same amount. The total stayed at 5.48 kg m/s.

The same total momentum is now carried by a bigger mass (0.58 kg instead of 0.41 kg), so the velocity must be smaller: 5.48 ÷ 0.58 = 9.4 m/s.

Quick check for any "join together" question: the final velocity must lie between the two starting velocities. If it doesn't, you have made a mistake.

understanding.intro: These aren't exam questions. They're the questions worth thinking about slowly, because they attack the misconceptions that make exam questions go wrong. Try each one properly before opening the answer.

questions.promptHtml:
Airbags are safety devices used in cars. In a crash, a driver of mass 65 kg is moving at 15 m/s.

(a) State the formula linking momentum, mass and velocity. (1)
(b) Calculate the momentum of the driver. (2)
(c) The airbag brings the driver to rest in 0.25 s. Calculate the average force on the driver. (2)
(d) Explain how the airbag reduces the force on the driver. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) momentum = mass × velocity 1

(b) 65 × 15 1

= 975 kg m/s 1

(c) force = change in momentum ÷ time taken = 975 ÷ 0.25 1

= 3900 N 1

(d) The airbag increases the time taken for the driver to stop 1

So the rate of change of momentum is smaller, and the force is smaller 1

This is the January 2022 question with new numbers. If your (b) was wrong, you would still get (c) for dividing your own answer by 0.25. Always carry on.

markScheme.point: (a) momentum = mass × velocity
= 975 kg m/s
(c) force = change in momentum ÷ time taken = 975 ÷ 0.25
(d) The airbag increases the time taken for the driver to stop
So the rate of change of momentum is smaller, and the force is smaller

questions.promptHtml:
(a) Which of these is the correct unit for momentum? (1)

A kg/m/s    B kg m/s²    C kg m/s    D kg² m/s

(b) State the principle of conservation of momentum. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) C, kg m/s 1

(b) The total momentum before a collision (or explosion) equals the total momentum after it, in the absence of external forces 1

B is the unit of force (a newton). Build the unit from p = m × v: kg × m/s.

markScheme.point: (a) C, kg m/s
(b) The total momentum before a collision (or explosion) equals the total momentum after it, in the absence of external forces

questions.promptHtml:
A hawk of mass 0.60 kg flies horizontally at 12 m/s. It catches a pigeon of mass 0.30 kg flying in the same direction at 3.0 m/s. After the catch they move together.

(a) Calculate the momentum of the hawk before the catch. (2)
(b) Calculate the total momentum of the two birds before the catch. (1)
(c) State the total momentum of the two birds just after the catch. (1)
(d) Calculate the velocity of the two birds just after the catch. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 0.60 × 12 1 = 7.2 kg m/s 1

(b) 7.2 + (0.30 × 3.0) = 7.2 + 0.90 = 8.1 kg m/s 1

(c) 8.1 kg m/s — the same as before, because momentum is conserved 1

(d) Total mass = 0.60 + 0.30 = 0.90 kg 1

velocity = 8.1 ÷ 0.90 1

= 9.0 m/s in the original direction 1

Modelled on 2023 Edexcel 2P Q4. Check: 9.0 m/s lies between 3.0 and 12 m/s, as it must.

markScheme.point: (c) 8.1 kg m/s — the same as before, because momentum is conserved
(d) Total mass = 0.60 + 0.30 = 0.90 kg
velocity = 8.1 ÷ 0.90
= 9.0 m/s in the original direction

questions.promptHtml:
Two trolleys, A and B, are at rest with a compressed spring between them. The spring is released. Trolley A (mass 1.5 kg) moves to the left at 2.0 m/s. Trolley B has a mass of 0.75 kg.

(a) Explain why the total momentum of the trolleys after the spring is released is zero. (1)
(b) Calculate the velocity of trolley B. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) The trolleys start at rest, so the total momentum before is zero, and momentum is conserved 1

(b) Taking right as positive: 0 = (1.5 × −2.0) + (0.75 × v) 1

0.75v = 3.0, so v = 3.0 ÷ 0.75 1

= 4.0 m/s to the right 1

The lighter trolley moves off faster, in the opposite direction. Its momentum (+3.0 kg m/s) is equal and opposite to A's (−3.0 kg m/s).

markScheme.point: (a) The trolleys start at rest, so the total momentum before is zero, and momentum is conserved
(b) Taking right as positive: 0 = (1.5 × −2.0) + (0.75 × v)
= 4.0 m/s to the right

questions.promptHtml:
An egg is dropped from the same height onto a hard floor and onto a thick carpet. It breaks on the floor but not on the carpet.

Explain why, using ideas about momentum. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
The carpet increases the time taken for the egg to stop (the impact time) 1

The egg's change in momentum is the same, so the rate of change of momentum is smaller 1

So the force on the egg is smaller 1

From 2022 Edexcel 2P Q2(c): the scheme wanted the impact time and the rate of change of momentum. "The carpet is soft" scores nothing without them.

markScheme.point: The carpet increases the time taken for the egg to stop (the impact time)
The egg's change in momentum is the same, so the rate of change of momentum is smaller
So the force on the egg is smaller

questions.promptHtml:
A tennis ball of mass 58 g is at rest. A racket hits it, and it leaves the racket at 50 m/s. The racket is in contact with the ball for 0.0040 s.

(a) Calculate the change in momentum of the ball. (2)
(b) Calculate the average force of the racket on the ball. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 58 g = 0.058 kg, so change in momentum = 0.058 × 50 − 0 1

= 2.9 kg m/s 1

(b) F = change in momentum ÷ t = 2.9 ÷ 0.0040 1

= 725 N (about 730 N) 1

Using 58 instead of 0.058 gives an answer a thousand times too big. Convert grams to kilograms first.

markScheme.point: (a) 58 g = 0.058 kg, so change in momentum = 0.058 × 50 − 0
= 2.9 kg m/s
(b) F = change in momentum ÷ t = 2.9 ÷ 0.0040
= 725 N (about 730 N)

questions.promptHtml:
A ball of mass 0.20 kg hits a wall at 8.0 m/s and bounces straight back at 6.0 m/s. It is in contact with the wall for 0.050 s.

(a) Calculate the size of the change in momentum of the ball. (3)
(b) Calculate the average force exerted on the ball by the wall. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Taking towards the wall as positive, momentum before = 0.20 × 8.0 = +1.6 kg m/s 1

Momentum after = 0.20 × (−6.0) = −1.2 kg m/s 1

Change = −1.2 − 1.6, so the size is 2.8 kg m/s 1

(b) F = 2.8 ÷ 0.050 1

= 56 N, directed away from the wall 1

0.4 kg m/s is the answer you get if you forget the ball has changed direction. The sizes of the two momenta add when the directions are opposite.

markScheme.point: (a) Taking towards the wall as positive, momentum before = 0.20 × 8.0 = +1.6 kg m/s
Momentum after = 0.20 × (−6.0) = −1.2 kg m/s
Change = −1.2 − 1.6, so the size is 2.8 kg m/s
= 56 N, directed away from the wall

questions.promptHtml:
Modern cars have crumple zones at the front and back.

Explain how a crumple zone reduces the risk of injury to the people in the car during a collision. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
The crumple zone deforms (crumples), which increases the time taken for the car and its passengers to stop 1

The change in momentum of the passengers is the same (they still go from their speed to zero) 1

So the rate of change of momentum is smaller 1

So the force on the passengers is smaller, and they are less likely to be injured 1

The script is always the same: time up, rate of change of momentum down, force down. Only the first line changes from feature to feature.

markScheme.point: The crumple zone deforms (crumples), which increases the time taken for the car and its passengers to stop
The change in momentum of the passengers is the same (they still go from their speed to zero)
So the rate of change of momentum is smaller
So the force on the passengers is smaller, and they are less likely to be injured

questions.promptHtml:
Trolley A of mass 2.0 kg moves to the right at 3.0 m/s. Trolley B of mass 1.0 kg moves to the left at 2.0 m/s. They collide head-on and stick together.

Calculate the velocity of the trolleys after the collision. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Taking right as positive, momentum of B = 1.0 × (−2.0) = −2.0 kg m/s 1

Total momentum before = 2.0 × 3.0 + (−2.0) = 4.0 kg m/s 1

velocity after = 4.0 ÷ (2.0 + 1.0) 1

= 1.3 m/s to the right 1

If you got 2.7 m/s, you added 6.0 and 2.0. B is moving the other way, so its momentum is negative.

markScheme.point: Taking right as positive, momentum of B = 1.0 × (−2.0) = −2.0 kg m/s
Total momentum before = 2.0 × 3.0 + (−2.0) = 4.0 kg m/s
velocity after = 4.0 ÷ (2.0 + 1.0)
= 1.3 m/s to the right

questions.promptHtml:
A rifle of mass 4.0 kg fires a bullet of mass 0.010 kg. The bullet leaves the rifle at 400 m/s.

(a) Calculate the momentum of the bullet. (2)
(b) Explain why the rifle moves backwards when the bullet is fired. (2)
(c) Calculate the recoil velocity of the rifle. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 0.010 × 400 1 = 4.0 kg m/s 1

(b) Before firing, the total momentum is zero 1

Momentum is conserved, so the rifle must have momentum equal in size and opposite in direction to the bullet's 1

(c) v = 4.0 ÷ 4.0 1

= 1.0 m/s backwards (opposite to the bullet) 1

The rifle is 400 times heavier than the bullet, so it moves 400 times more slowly.

markScheme.point: (b) Before firing, the total momentum is zero
Momentum is conserved, so the rifle must have momentum equal in size and opposite in direction to the bullet's
= 1.0 m/s backwards (opposite to the bullet)

questions.promptHtml:
Two ice skaters stand at rest facing each other, then push apart. Skater A has a mass of 60 kg and moves off at 2.0 m/s. Skater B moves off in the opposite direction at 3.0 m/s.

Calculate the mass of skater B. Ignore friction. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
Total momentum before = 0, so 0 = (60 × 2.0) + (m × −3.0) 1

3.0m = 120, so m = 120 ÷ 3.0 1

= 40 kg 1

Sense check: B moves faster, so B must be lighter. 40 kg is lighter than 60 kg.

markScheme.point: Total momentum before = 0, so 0 = (60 × 2.0) + (m × −3.0)
= 40 kg

questions.promptHtml:
A car of mass 1200 kg speeds up from 10 m/s to 25 m/s in 6.0 s.

(a) State the relationship between force, change in momentum and time taken. (1)
(b) Calculate the resultant force on the car. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) force = change in momentum ÷ time taken 1

(b) Change in momentum = (1200 × 25) − (1200 × 10) = 18 000 kg m/s 1

F = 18 000 ÷ 6.0 1

= 3000 N 1

Using only the final momentum (30 000 ÷ 6.0 = 5000 N) is the classic error. The car already had momentum before it sped up.

markScheme.point: (a) force = change in momentum ÷ time taken
(b) Change in momentum = (1200 × 25) − (1200 × 10) = 18 000 kg m/s

questions.promptHtml:
(a) Explain how a seat belt reduces the force on a passenger when a car stops suddenly. (3)
(b) A cycle helmet has a thick foam lining. Explain how the lining protects the rider's head in a fall. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) The seat belt stretches slightly, increasing the time taken for the passenger to stop 1

The passenger's change in momentum is the same, so the rate of change of momentum is smaller 1

So the force on the passenger is smaller 1

(b) The foam compresses, increasing the time taken for the head to stop 1

So the rate of change of momentum of the head, and the force on it, is smaller 1

"It is soft" or "it cushions the head" is not enough. Name the time and the force.

markScheme.point: (a) The seat belt stretches slightly, increasing the time taken for the passenger to stop
The passenger's change in momentum is the same, so the rate of change of momentum is smaller
So the force on the passenger is smaller
(b) The foam compresses, increasing the time taken for the head to stop
So the rate of change of momentum of the head, and the force on it, is smaller

questions.promptHtml:
A snooker ball of mass 0.16 kg moving at 2.5 m/s hits a stationary snooker ball of the same mass. After the collision the first ball moves on in the same direction at 0.50 m/s.

(a) Calculate the velocity of the second ball after the collision. (3)
(b) State one assumption you made in your calculation. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Total momentum before = 0.16 × 2.5 = 0.40 kg m/s 1

0.40 = (0.16 × 0.50) + (0.16 × v), so 0.16v = 0.32 1

v = 2.0 m/s in the original direction 1

(b) No external forces act on the balls during the collision (friction from the table is negligible) 1

The stationary ball has zero momentum before, but it still appears in the "after" side of the equation.

markScheme.point: (a) Total momentum before = 0.16 × 2.5 = 0.40 kg m/s
v = 2.0 m/s in the original direction
(b) No external forces act on the balls during the collision (friction from the table is negligible)

questions.promptHtml:
A car of mass 1500 kg travelling at 20 m/s crashes into a solid wall and stops.

(a) Calculate the momentum of the car just before the crash. (2)
(b) The car stops in 0.12 s. Calculate the average force on the car. (2)
(c) A car with a crumple zone stops in 0.30 s instead. Calculate the average force on this car. (2)
(d) A passenger of mass 70 kg wearing a seat belt stops in 0.30 s. Calculate the average force on the passenger. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 1500 × 20 1 = 30 000 kg m/s 1

(b) F = 30 000 ÷ 0.12 1 = 250 000 N 1

(c) F = 30 000 ÷ 0.30 1 = 100 000 N 1

(d) Change in momentum = 70 × 20 = 1400 kg m/s, so F = 1400 ÷ 0.30 1

= 4700 N (2 s.f.) 1

Compare (b) and (c): the same change in momentum, 2.5 times the time, so 2.5 times less force. That is the whole safety argument in numbers.

markScheme.point: (d) Change in momentum = 70 × 20 = 1400 kg m/s, so F = 1400 ÷ 0.30

drill.intro: Now in exam register. Time yourself at roughly one minute per mark. State formulas when asked, show substitutions, give units, and give a direction or a sign for every velocity and momentum.

modules.title: Light, Refraction and Total Internal Reflection
modules.standfirst: How light bounces off mirrors, bends at the edge of glass and water, and gets trapped inside optical fibres. The marks go to people who measure from the normal, take the sine before dividing, and give both conditions for total internal reflection. A Year 11 topic: taught in Year 11, for the GCSE in summer 2027.

intel.html:
This topic appeared in five of the ten real Edexcel papers checked, for 31 marks in total. It comes as one self-contained question of 5 to 8 marks, and the same three things keep returning: measure an angle with a protractor, state and use n = sin i ÷ sin r, and explain a path using refraction or total internal reflection.

PaperWhat was asked
2024 Edexcel 1P Q8 (6)Two rays hit an air/water boundary (n = 1.33). Explain both paths, with measured angles of incidence and calculated angles of refraction, and why there is no total internal reflection
2023 Edexcel 2P Q7(a) (6)Light entering a glass prism: name the protractor, measure i and r, state n = sin i ÷ sin r, calculate the refractive index (1.5)
2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q6 (6)Optical fibres: what waves transfer, draw the incident ray in air, name refraction, explain the path along the fibre (total internal reflection, denser core, angle above the critical angle)
2022 Edexcel Jan 1P Q4 (5)Plane mirror practical: name the protractor, label and measure the angle of incidence (79°), draw the reflected ray
2022 Edexcel Jan 1P Q10 (8)Violet light entering a prism: find r from an angle measured to the surface, state the formula, refractive index to 2 s.f., then deduce how refractive index depends on wavelength from red and violet rays

Two patterns are worth noticing. "State the formula linking refractive index, angle of incidence and angle of refraction" has been a free mark twice. And every one of these questions needs the normal: the angles are measured from it, and a diagram angle measured from the surface has to be taken away from 90° first.

On the formula sheet: the 2022–2024 June papers printed both refraction equations on their formula page. The current specification (Issue 4, 2024) lists them among the relationships that will not be provided. For 2027, learn both by heart.

On 2023 2P Q7, the mark scheme says: "reject division of i and r giving approx 1.5-1.6". Dividing the angles themselves (44 ÷ 28 = 1.57) looks right and scores nothing. You must take the sine of each angle first: sin 44° ÷ sin 28° = 1.48, which rounds to 1.5.

And on 2024 1P Q8, where some candidates worked out a critical angle for rays going from air into water: "ignore calculated values of the critical angle as not relevant". Total internal reflection cannot happen when light enters the denser material, so the critical angle has nothing to do with it.
