subsections.html: Module 04 introduced reflection and refraction as things all waves do. This module does it properly for light: the angles, the refractive index, the critical angle and total internal reflection. Every heading says where it was actually asked. All angles in this topic are measured from the normal, never from the surface.

subsections.heading: Light is a transverse wave that can be reflected and refracted
subsections.html:
Spec 3.14 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q6(a)

Light is a transverse wave, and like every wave it can be reflected and refracted. Transverse means the vibrations are at right angles to the direction the wave travels. That was module 04; here it is the starting point.

Light is part of the electromagnetic spectrum, so it travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum (and almost exactly that in air). It slows down when it enters glass, water or Perspex. That change of speed is what makes it bend.

2023 Jan 1P Q6(a) opened with a free mark: optical fibres use light to communicate, because waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter.

subsections.heading: The normal, and how to measure an angle
subsections.html:
Spec 3.15, 3.16 · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1P Q4(a), (b) · 2023 Edexcel 2P Q7(a)(i), (ii) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1P Q10(a)(i)

The normal is a line drawn at 90° to the surface at the point where the ray hits it, and every angle is measured from the normal. Draw it as a dashed line with a ruler.

  • The angle of incidence, i, is between the incident ray and the normal.
  • The angle of reflection is between the reflected ray and the normal.
  • The angle of refraction, r, is between the refracted ray and the normal.

The instrument that measures angles is a protractor. It has been a 1-mark question twice (2022 Jan 1P Q4(a), 2023 2P Q7(a)(i)).

The angle-to-the-surface trap. 2022 Jan 1P Q10 marked the refracted ray at 54° to the surface of the prism. The angle of refraction is 90° − 54° = 36°. Using 54° gives the wrong refractive index.

✗ "The angle of incidence is the angle between the ray and the mirror."
✓ "The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal."

When you measure, put the protractor's centre exactly on the point where the ray meets the surface, and line its zero up with the normal. The 2023 mark scheme allowed about ±2° either side, so careful measuring is part of the mark.

subsections.heading: Reflection and the plane mirror
subsections.html:
Spec 3.15, 3.16 · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1P Q4

The law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Both are measured from the normal, and the reflected ray is on the other side of the normal from the incident ray.

To draw the reflected ray, as 2022 Jan 1P Q4(b)(iii) asked for 2 marks:

  1. Draw the normal at the point where the ray hits the mirror.
  2. Measure the angle of incidence (79° on that paper).
  3. On the other side of the normal, starting from the same point, draw a straight ray at the same angle to the normal. Add an arrow pointing away from the mirror.

The two marks were for a straight ray on the correct side of the normal coming from the point of incidence, and for the correct angle.

The mirror practical

Put the plane mirror on paper and draw along its back. Draw a normal. Shine a narrow ray from a ray box at the point where the normal meets the mirror. Mark the incident and reflected rays with two crosses each, then join the crosses with a ruler. Measure both angles from the normal with a protractor. Repeat for several angles of incidence. Each time, angle of incidence = angle of reflection.

subsections.heading: Refraction: which way does the ray bend?
subsections.html:
Spec 3.14, 3.16 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q6(b) · 2024 Edexcel 1P Q8

Refraction is the change in direction of light as it crosses from one material into another, because its speed changes.

Light goesSpeedBendsSo
From air into glass or waterSlows downTowards the normalr is smaller than i
From glass or water out into airSpeeds upAway from the normalThe angle in air is larger
Along the normal (i = 0°)Still changesDoes not bendGoes straight through

A material in which light travels more slowly is called optically denser. Glass and water are optically denser than air. The 2024 mark scheme gave a mark for "water and air have different (optical) densities" and another for "light travels slower in water than air".

2023 Jan 1P Q6(b) showed the refracted ray inside the glass and asked for the ray in air before it hit the boundary. The mark needed the ray in air to be further from the normal than the ray in the glass, because the ray bends towards the normal as it goes in.

2023 Jan 1P Q6(b)(ii) asked for the name of the behaviour. The mark scheme accepted any recognisable spelling of refraction but said "reject if spelling implies reflection". Write it clearly.

✗ "The light bends because the glass is thicker."
✓ "The light slows down as it enters the glass, so it changes direction towards the normal."

subsections.heading: Ray diagrams through blocks
subsections.html:
Spec 3.16, 3.17

A ray through a rectangular glass block bends towards the normal going in, away from the normal coming out, and leaves parallel to the ray that went in.

  1. At the first face: air to glass, so the ray bends towards the normal.
  2. Inside the block: a straight line to the opposite face.
  3. At the second face: glass to air, so it bends away from the normal by the same amount.
  4. Because the two faces are parallel, the emerging ray is parallel to the incident ray, just shifted sideways.

Rules for drawing that earn the marks: use a ruler, draw a normal at every point where the ray meets a surface, put arrows on the rays, and make the bend go the right way at each face. Some light is also reflected at each surface. Examiners do not need it unless they ask; the 2024 scheme said "ignore reflected rays".

subsections.heading: Refractive index: n = sin i ÷ sin r
subsections.html:
Spec 3.18 · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1P Q10(a)(ii), (iii) · 2023 Edexcel 2P Q7(a)(iii), (iv) · 2024 Edexcel 1P Q8

The refractive index of a material tells you how much it bends light: n = sin i ÷ sin r.

n = sin i ÷ sin r
n = refractive index (no unit) · i = angle of incidence in air (°) · r = angle of refraction in the material (°)

Three facts about n. It has no unit, because it is one sine divided by another. It is always greater than 1 for glass, water or Perspex, because light slows down and bends towards the normal, so sin i is bigger than sin r. And a bigger n means the light bends more. Typical values: water 1.33, glass about 1.5.

Mark script: calculate the refractive index

From 2022 Jan 1P Q10, three marks: substitution, evaluation, answer to 2 s.f.

i = 61°, and the refracted ray was at 54° to the surface, so r = 90 − 54 = 36°.

n = sin 61° ÷ sin 36° = 0.875 ÷ 0.588 = 1.488… = 1.5 (2 s.f.)

Using it the other way round (2024 1P Q8): water has n = 1.33 and a ray hits it at i = 36°. Then sin r = sin 36° ÷ 1.33 = 0.442, so r = 26°. The scheme accepted 24°–28°.

✗ n = 44 ÷ 28 = 1.57  — "reject division of i and r giving approx 1.5-1.6"
✓ n = sin 44° ÷ sin 28° = 0.695 ÷ 0.469 = 1.48 = 1.5

Check your calculator is in degrees (a small D on the screen). In radians, sin 44 gives 0.018 and everything after it is wrong.

If the light is coming out of the glass, i in the equation is still the angle in air and r is still the angle in the glass. The angle in air is always the bigger one.

subsections.heading: Practical: the refractive index of a glass block
subsections.html:
Spec 3.17, 3.19

Trace rays through a rectangular glass block, measure i and r from the normal, and calculate n = sin i ÷ sin r for several angles.

  1. Put the block on a sheet of paper and draw around it with a sharp pencil.
  2. Draw a normal at a point on one long side.
  3. Use a ray box with a narrow slit to aim a ray at that point, at a measured angle of incidence, e.g. 20°.
  4. Mark the ray that comes out of the far side with two crosses, well apart.
  5. Remove the block. Join the crosses and extend back to the block's outline. Join the point where the ray went in to the point where it came out. That line is the refracted ray inside the glass.
  6. Measure the angle of refraction, r, from the normal with a protractor.
  7. Repeat for a range of angles of incidence, e.g. 20°, 30°, 40°, 50°, 60°.
  8. Calculate sin i ÷ sin r for each and take the mean. Or plot sin i against sin r: a straight line through the origin whose gradient is n.

Why these details matter: a narrow ray and crosses far apart make the line more accurate. A darkened room makes the ray easier to see. Several angles and a mean reduce the effect of small measuring errors. A typical result for glass is about 1.5.

subsections.heading: Prisms, semi-circular blocks, and colours
subsections.html:
Spec 3.17 · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1P Q10(b) · 2023 Edexcel 2P Q7(a)

A triangular prism bends light at both faces it passes through, and because the faces are not parallel the ray comes out in a new direction. The rule at each face is the same as for the block: towards the normal going in, away from the normal coming out.

A semi-circular block is used to study light leaving glass. Aim the ray at the centre of the flat face, through the curved side. The ray then enters the curved side along a radius, which is along the normal, so it does not bend going in. All the bending happens at the flat face, where you can measure it. This is how you find the critical angle (next section).

2022 Jan 1P Q10(b) shows why prisms make rainbows. White light is a mixture of colours. Glass has a slightly different refractive index for each colour, so each colour bends by a different amount and the colours spread out. The mark scheme wanted three linked points:

  1. Red refracts less than violet.
  2. So red has a lower refractive index than violet.
  3. Red has a longer wavelength, so refractive index decreases as wavelength increases.

subsections.heading: The critical angle
subsections.html:
Spec 3.21 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q6(c)

The critical angle is the angle of incidence, inside the denser material, at which the angle of refraction is 90°. At that angle the refracted ray skims along the boundary.

What you see with a semi-circular block as you increase the angle of incidence at the flat face:

  1. Small angles: most light refracts out into the air, bending away from the normal. A weak ray is also reflected back inside.
  2. Increasing the angle: the refracted ray bends further from the normal and gets dimmer; the reflected ray gets brighter.
  3. At the critical angle: the refracted ray travels along the boundary, at 90° to the normal.
  4. Above the critical angle: no light leaves. All of it is reflected back inside. This is total internal reflection.

Critical angles: about 42° for glass (n = 1.5) and about 49° for water (n = 1.33). A higher refractive index gives a smaller critical angle.

subsections.heading: Total internal reflection: the two conditions
subsections.html:
Spec 3.20, 3.21 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q6(c) · 2024 Edexcel 1P Q8

Total internal reflection happens only when both conditions are met: light is going from a denser material into a less dense one, and the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.

  1. The light is travelling from a more optically dense material to a less dense one (higher to lower refractive index), e.g. glass to air or water to air.
  2. The angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.

Then all of the light reflects back inside, obeying the law of reflection.

Mark script: "explain the paths of the rays" (2024 1P Q8, 6 marks)

Two rays from a lamp in air hit a water surface (n = 1.33). The six marks, any six from seven:

  • Ray A is refracted and changes direction.
  • Ray B is refracted and changes direction.
  • A correctly measured angle of incidence: about 36° for A, 60° for B.
  • A correctly calculated angle of refraction: sin 36° ÷ 1.33 gives 26°; sin 60° ÷ 1.33 gives 41°.
  • Water and air have different optical densities.
  • Light travels slower in water than in air.
  • No total internal reflection, because the light is going into the denser material.

Draw both refracted rays, bending towards the normal, on the diagram. The question said "include calculations"; do them for both rays.

✗ "The ray is totally internally reflected because the angle is big."
✓ "The ray is totally internally reflected because it is going from glass into air and the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle."

Light going from air into water or glass can never be totally internally reflected, however steep the angle. The scheme said to "ignore calculated values of the critical angle as not relevant" in that situation.

subsections.heading: Critical angle and refractive index: sin c = 1 ÷ n
subsections.html:
Spec 3.22

The critical angle depends only on the refractive index: sin c = 1 ÷ n.

sin c = 1 ÷ n
c = critical angle (°), measured from the normal inside the denser material · n = refractive index of that material (no unit)

Mark script: both directions

Find c from n. Glass, n = 1.50: sin c = 1 ÷ 1.50 = 0.667. c = sin⁻¹ 0.667 = 41.8° = 42°.

Find n from c. A student measures c = 43° with a semi-circular block: n = 1 ÷ sin 43° = 1 ÷ 0.682 = 1.466 = 1.47.

Show three steps: the equation, the substitution, the answer. The last step needs the sin⁻¹ (shift sin) button.

✗ sin c = 1 ÷ 1.50 = 0.667, so c = 0.667°
✓ sin c = 0.667, so c = sin⁻¹ 0.667 = 42°

The number 0.667 is the sine of the angle, not the angle. And a critical angle must be less than 90°; if you get something bigger, you have divided the wrong way round.

subsections.heading: Optical fibres and prisms that reflect
subsections.html:
Spec 3.20 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q6

An optical fibre carries light along its length by total internal reflection, many times over.

  1. Light enters one end of the thin glass fibre, refracting as it goes in.
  2. It hits the side of the fibre at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.
  3. The glass core is optically denser than what surrounds it, so the light is totally internally reflected.
  4. This repeats all along the fibre, even round gentle bends, so the light reaches the far end with very little lost.

The 3-mark answer to 2023 Jan 1P Q6(c) was exactly those three words: total internal reflection; because the core has a higher refractive index than air; because the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle. Uses: sending information (telephone and internet signals) as pulses of light, and endoscopes that let doctors see inside the body.

Prisms use the same effect. In a glass prism with angles of 45°, 45° and 90°, light enters one short face along the normal, so it does not bend. It then meets the long face at 45°. That is greater than the critical angle of glass (42°), so the light is totally internally reflected. The ray turns through 90°, as in a periscope, or through 180° using two reflections, as in binoculars and bicycle reflectors. Almost all the light is reflected, which is better than a mirror.

✗ "The light bounces off the sides of the fibre."
✓ "The light is totally internally reflected at the sides of the fibre, because the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle."

"Bounces" and "reflects" earn nothing on their own. You need the full name and the reason.

subsections.heading: Sound waves reflect and refract too
subsections.html:
Spec 3.23

Sound waves are longitudinal, and they can also be reflected and refracted. Module 04 covers sound in detail. Only three points belong here.

  • Sound is longitudinal: the vibrations are parallel to the direction the wave travels. Light is transverse.
  • A reflected sound is an echo. Sonar and ultrasound scanning use reflected sound.
  • Sound is refracted when it changes speed as it passes into a new material. It goes the opposite way from light: sound speeds up going from air into water, so it bends away from the normal.

The sentences behind most of the marks

Every angle is measured from the normal, a line at 90° to the surface. The instrument is a protractor.

Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection.

Refraction: light changes speed at a boundary, so it changes direction. Into glass or water it slows and bends towards the normal; out into air it bends away.

n = sin i ÷ sin r: take the sines before dividing. No unit. Glass about 1.5, water 1.33.

Total internal reflection needs both: light going from a denser to a less dense material, and the angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.

Optical fibres and 45° prisms work by total internal reflection. Glass: c ≈ 42°, and 45° is bigger.

subsections.heading: Equations
subsections.html:
Both must be learnt by heart. The current specification says they will not be given on the formula sheet.

Refractive index — memorisen = sin i ÷ sin rn = refractive index (no unit) · i = angle of incidence in air (°) · r = angle of refraction in the material (°) · both measured from the normal
Critical angle — memorisesin c = 1 ÷ nc = critical angle (°), measured from the normal inside the denser material · n = refractive index of that material (no unit) · use sin⁻¹ to get c

questions.promptHtml: A ray of light hits a glass block at an angle and bends. A second ray hits the block along the normal and goes straight on. Both rays slow down. Why does only one of them bend?
questions.hint: Which side of a wide beam reaches the glass first?
questions.answerHtml:
Picture the ray as a wide beam with a straight front. If it arrives at an angle, one side of the front enters the glass first and slows down, while the other side is still in air, moving fast. The fast side catches up, so the whole front swings round. That swing is the change of direction.

If the beam arrives along the normal, the whole front enters the glass at the same moment. It all slows together, so nothing swings round. The speed changes; the direction does not.

The point: refraction is caused by the change of speed, but you only see a change of direction when the light meets the boundary at an angle.

questions.promptHtml: Why does refractive index have no unit, and why is it always more than 1 for glass or water?
questions.answerHtml:
No unit: n = sin i ÷ sin r. A sine is a ratio of two lengths and has no unit, so one sine divided by another has no unit either.

More than 1: light slows down in glass or water, so it bends towards the normal. That makes r smaller than i, so sin r is smaller than sin i, and sin i ÷ sin r is bigger than 1.

Use it as a check: if you calculate a refractive index of 0.67, you have divided the wrong way round. If you give it a unit, you lose the mark.

questions.promptHtml: A student measures i = 44° and r = 28° and writes n = 44 ÷ 28 = 1.57. The answer looks sensible for glass. Why does the mark scheme reject it?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the equation uses the sines of the angles, and sine is not proportional to the angle. Doubling an angle does not double its sine.

Correctly: n = sin 44° ÷ sin 28° = 0.695 ÷ 0.469 = 1.48, which is 1.5 to 2 s.f.

The two answers are close here only by luck. Try i = 70° and r = 39°: dividing the angles gives 1.79, but sin 70° ÷ sin 39° = 1.49. The 2023 scheme said "reject division of i and r giving approx 1.5-1.6", so the examiners were ready for exactly this mistake.

questions.promptHtml: Why can light going from air into water never be totally internally reflected, however steep the angle?
questions.hint: Which way does the ray bend going into water?
questions.answerHtml:
Going from air into water, light slows down and bends towards the normal. So the angle of refraction is always smaller than the angle of incidence. Even at an angle of incidence of almost 90°, the refracted ray is only at about 49° to the normal.

Total internal reflection needs the refracted ray to reach 90° and have nowhere to go. That can only happen when the ray bends away from the normal, which means going from the denser material to the less dense one.

This was the seventh mark point on 2024 1P Q8: no total internal reflection, because water is more optically dense than air.

questions.promptHtml: Show that sin c = 1 ÷ n follows from n = sin i ÷ sin r.
questions.answerHtml:
In n = sin i ÷ sin r, i is the angle in air and r is the angle in the glass, whichever way the light travels.

At the critical angle, light leaving the glass meets the boundary at c (inside the glass) and leaves at 90° in air. So the angle in air is 90° and the angle in glass is c:

n = sin 90° ÷ sin c = 1 ÷ sin c, so sin c = 1 ÷ n.

What it tells you: the bigger the refractive index, the smaller the critical angle, and the easier it is to trap light by total internal reflection.

questions.promptHtml: A ray passes through a rectangular glass block and comes out parallel to the ray that went in. Why parallel? And why does a triangular prism not do the same?
questions.answerHtml:
In a rectangular block the two faces are parallel, so their normals are parallel too. The ray meets the second face at the same angle it was refracted to at the first face. Coming out, it bends away from the normal by exactly as much as it bent towards the normal going in. The two bends cancel, so the ray leaves in its original direction, just shifted sideways.

In a triangular prism the two faces are at an angle to each other. Their normals point in different directions, so the two bends do not cancel. Both bends turn the ray the same way, towards the thick base of the prism, so it leaves in a new direction.

questions.promptHtml: White light goes into a prism and comes out as a spread of colours, with violet bent the most and red the least. What does this tell you about the refractive index of glass?
questions.answerHtml:
Every colour hits the prism at the same angle of incidence. Violet is bent the most, so its angle of refraction is the smallest, and from n = sin i ÷ sin r its refractive index is the largest. Red is bent the least, so it has the smallest refractive index.

Red has a longer wavelength than violet. So for glass, refractive index decreases as wavelength increases.

That is exactly the 3-mark chain on 2022 Jan 1P Q10(b): red refracts less than violet; so red has a lower refractive index; so refractive index decreases with increasing wavelength.

questions.promptHtml: An optical fibre still carries light round a gentle curve. Explain why, and explain what could happen if it were bent very sharply.
questions.answerHtml:
Round a gentle curve, the light still meets the side of the fibre at a large angle to the normal, greater than the critical angle. So it is still totally internally reflected, and it follows the fibre round.

At a very sharp bend, the side of the fibre turns towards the light. The light then meets the side more nearly along the normal, so its angle of incidence gets smaller. If it falls below the critical angle, the light refracts out through the side and escapes, and the signal is weakened.

The point: total internal reflection is not a property of the fibre alone. It depends on the angle every time the light meets the boundary.

(a) Protractor 1

(b) The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection 1

questions.promptHtml:
A ray of violet light enters a glass prism with an angle of incidence of 60°. Inside the prism, the refracted ray makes an angle of 55° with the surface of the prism.

(a) (i) Calculate the angle of refraction. (1)
(ii) State the formula linking refractive index, angle of incidence and angle of refraction. (1)
(iii) Calculate the refractive index of the prism for violet light. Give your answer to 2 significant figures. (3)
(b) Red light enters the prism at the same angle and is refracted less than the violet light. Red light has a longer wavelength than violet light. Deduce a possible relationship between the wavelength and the refractive index for colours of visible light. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a)(i) 90 − 55 = 35° 1

(ii) refractive index = sin(angle of incidence) ÷ sin(angle of refraction), n = sin i ÷ sin r 1

(iii) n = sin 60° ÷ sin 35° 1

= 0.866 ÷ 0.574 = 1.509… 1

= 1.5 (2 s.f.) 1

(b) Red refracts less than violet 1

So red light has a lower refractive index than violet light 1

So the refractive index decreases as the wavelength increases 1

Modelled on 2022 Jan 1P Q10, which also gave the refracted ray's angle to the surface. Subtract from 90° first.

markScheme.point: (ii) refractive index = sin(angle of incidence) ÷ sin(angle of refraction), n = sin i ÷ sin r
(iii) n = sin 60° ÷ sin 35°
(b) Red refracts less than violet
So red light has a lower refractive index than violet light
So the refractive index decreases as the wavelength increases

questions.promptHtml:
Two rays of light, A and B, travel from a lamp in air and strike the flat surface of a pond. Ray A has an angle of incidence of 30°. Ray B has an angle of incidence of 55°. The refractive index of water is 1.33.

Explain the paths of the two rays after they strike the boundary between air and water. Include calculations in your answer. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Ray A is refracted: it changes direction, bending towards the normal 1

Ray B is also refracted, bending towards the normal 1

Ray A: sin r = sin 30° ÷ 1.33 = 0.376, so r = 22° 1

Ray B: sin r = sin 55° ÷ 1.33 = 0.616, so r = 38° 1

Light travels more slowly in water than in air; water is optically denser 1

There is no total internal reflection, because the light is going into the denser material 1

Modelled on 2024 1P Q8. The scheme said to "ignore calculated values of the critical angle as not relevant". Working out 49° for water here wastes time and earns nothing.

markScheme.point: Ray A is refracted: it changes direction, bending towards the normal
Ray B is also refracted, bending towards the normal
Ray A: sin r = sin 30° ÷ 1.33 = 0.376, so r = 22°
Ray B: sin r = sin 55° ÷ 1.33 = 0.616, so r = 38°
Light travels more slowly in water than in air; water is optically denser
There is no total internal reflection, because the light is going into the denser material

questions.promptHtml:
This question is about optical fibres.

(a) Optical fibres use light waves for communication. State what waves transfer, and what they do not transfer. (1)
(b) A ray of light passes from air into the end of a glass optical fibre. State the name of the wave behaviour that changes its direction at this boundary. (1)
(c) Explain the path of the ray of light as it travels along the optical fibre. (3)
(d) The glass has a refractive index of 1.52. Calculate its critical angle. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter 1

(b) Refraction 1

(c) The light is totally internally reflected at the sides of the fibre 1

Because the glass core has a higher refractive index than the material around it (it is optically denser) 1

And because the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle 1

(d) sin c = 1 ÷ n 1

sin c = 1 ÷ 1.52 = 0.658 1

c = sin⁻¹ 0.658 = 41° 1

Modelled on 2023 Jan 1P Q6. In (b), spell it so it cannot be read as "reflection": the scheme rejected that.

markScheme.point: (a) Waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter
(b) Refraction
(c) The light is totally internally reflected at the sides of the fibre
Because the glass core has a higher refractive index than the material around it (it is optically denser)
And because the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle
(d) sin c = 1 ÷ n

questions.promptHtml:
A student shines a ray into a glass prism and measures an angle of incidence of 50° and an angle of refraction of 31°.

(a) State the formula linking refractive index, angle of incidence and angle of refraction. (1)
(b) Calculate the refractive index of the glass. (2)
(c) Another student writes 50 ÷ 31 = 1.6. Explain why this is wrong. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) n = sin i ÷ sin r 1

(b) n = sin 50° ÷ sin 31° 1

= 0.766 ÷ 0.515 = 1.5 (1.49) 1

(c) The formula uses the sines of the angles; the angles themselves cannot be divided 1

2023 2P Q7: "reject division of i and r giving approx 1.5-1.6".

markScheme.point: (a) n = sin i ÷ sin r
(b) n = sin 50° ÷ sin 31°
(c) The formula uses the sines of the angles; the angles themselves cannot be divided

questions.promptHtml: Describe an experiment to determine the refractive index of glass using a rectangular glass block. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Place the block on paper, draw around it, and draw a normal at a point on one side 1

Use a ray box to direct a narrow ray at that point, at a measured angle of incidence 1

Mark the path of the ray leaving the block with crosses, then remove the block 1

Join the point where the ray entered to the point where it left, to show the refracted ray inside the block 1

Measure the angle of refraction from the normal with a protractor 1

Repeat for several angles of incidence, calculate sin i ÷ sin r each time and find the mean (or plot sin i against sin r; the gradient is n) 1

Also creditable in place of one of the above: use a darkened room; mark crosses far apart; measure angles from the normal, not the surface.

Use a ray box to direct a narrow ray at that point, at a measured angle of incidence

(a) Explain what is meant by the critical angle. (2)
(b) State the formula linking critical angle and refractive index. (1)
(c) The critical angle of a Perspex block is 42°. Calculate the refractive index of Perspex. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) The angle of incidence in the denser material 1

For which the angle of refraction is 90° (the refracted ray travels along the boundary) 1

(b) sin c = 1 ÷ n 1

(c) n = 1 ÷ sin 42° = 1 ÷ 0.669 1

= 1.49 1

markScheme.point: (a) The angle of incidence in the denser material
For which the angle of refraction is 90° (the refracted ray travels along the boundary)
(b) sin c = 1 ÷ n

questions.promptHtml:
Light travels inside a glass block of refractive index 1.50 towards the glass/air boundary.

(a) Calculate the critical angle for this glass. (3)
(b) State what happens to the light when its angle of incidence at the boundary is (i) 30° and (ii) 60°. (2)
(c) Explain why light travelling from air into the glass can never be totally internally reflected. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) sin c = 1 ÷ n = 1 ÷ 1.50 1

sin c = 0.667 1

c = sin⁻¹ 0.667 = 42° (41.8°) 1

(b)(i) 30° is less than the critical angle, so the light refracts out into the air, bending away from the normal 1

(ii) 60° is greater than the critical angle, so the light is totally internally reflected 1

(c) Total internal reflection needs light going from a denser to a less dense material; going into glass the light bends towards the normal 1

markScheme.point: sin c = 0.667
(b)(i) 30° is less than the critical angle, so the light refracts out into the air, bending away from the normal
(ii) 60° is greater than the critical angle, so the light is totally internally reflected
(c) Total internal reflection needs light going from a denser to a less dense material; going into glass the light bends towards the normal

questions.promptHtml:
A periscope uses two glass prisms with angles of 45°, 45° and 90°. Light enters one short face of a prism at 90° to that face. The critical angle of the glass is 42°.

Explain why the prism turns the light through 90°. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
The light enters along the normal, so it does not change direction 1

It meets the long face with an angle of incidence of 45° 1

45° is greater than the critical angle of 42° (and the light is going from glass to air) 1

So it is totally internally reflected at 45° to the normal, turning through 90° 1

It meets the long face with an angle of incidence of 45°
45° is greater than the critical angle of 42° (and the light is going from glass to air)
So it is totally internally reflected at 45° to the normal, turning through 90°

questions.promptHtml:
A ray of light strikes a plane mirror. The angle between the incident ray and the mirror is 30°.

(a) State the angle of incidence. (1)
(b) State the angle of reflection. (1)
(c) Calculate the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 90 − 30 = 60° 1

(b) 60°, equal to the angle of incidence 1

(c) 60 + 60 = 120° 1

Sketch it. The two rays sit either side of the normal, so the angle between them is the sum of the two angles.

markScheme.point: (b) 60°, equal to the angle of incidence

questions.promptHtml:
A ray of light in air strikes a glass block with an angle of incidence of 40°. The refractive index of the glass is 1.5.

(a) Calculate the angle of refraction. (3)
(b) A second ray strikes the block along the normal. State its angle of refraction. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) sin r = sin i ÷ n = sin 40° ÷ 1.5 1

sin r = 0.643 ÷ 1.5 = 0.429 1

r = sin⁻¹ 0.429 = 25° 1

(b) 0°: it passes straight through without changing direction 1

Check: r is smaller than i, as it must be for light entering glass.

(b) 0°: it passes straight through without changing direction

questions.promptHtml:
A ray of light enters one long side of a rectangular glass block at an angle and leaves through the opposite side.

Describe the path of the ray, as it would be shown on a ray diagram. (3)

On entering the glass it bends towards the normal 1

On leaving the glass it bends away from the normal 1

It leaves parallel to the incident ray, shifted sideways 1

On a diagram: ruler, a normal at both points, arrows on every ray.

On leaving the glass it bends away from the normal

(a) A person shouts towards a cliff and hears an echo. Name the wave behaviour that causes the echo. (1)
(b) Sound travels faster in water than in air. A sound wave passes from air into water at an angle. State and explain which way it bends. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Reflection 1

(b) It bends away from the normal 1

Because it speeds up as it enters the water, so it is refracted the opposite way to light 1

markScheme.point: (a) Reflection
(b) It bends away from the normal
Because it speeds up as it enters the water, so it is refracted the opposite way to light

questions.promptHtml:
A student uses a semi-circular glass block to find the critical angle of glass. A ray is directed through the curved side at the centre of the flat side.

(a) Explain why the ray does not change direction as it enters the curved side. (1)
(b) The student slowly increases the angle of incidence at the flat side. Describe what is seen. (3)
(c) The student measures the critical angle as 43°. Calculate the refractive index of the glass. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) It enters along a radius, which is along the normal to the curved surface 1

(b) The refracted ray bends further from the normal and gets dimmer, while the reflected ray gets brighter 1

At the critical angle, the refracted ray travels along the flat surface (angle of refraction 90°) 1

Above the critical angle, all the light is reflected back inside: total internal reflection 1

(c) sin c = 1 ÷ n, so n = 1 ÷ sin c 1

n = 1 ÷ sin 43° = 1 ÷ 0.682 1

= 1.47 1

(b) The refracted ray bends further from the normal and gets dimmer, while the reflected ray gets brighter

Above the critical angle, all the light is reflected back inside: total internal reflection

questions.promptHtml:
Full exam-style question. A lamp sits at the bottom of a swimming pool. The refractive index of water is 1.33.

(a) Calculate the critical angle for water. (3)
(b) A ray from the lamp meets the water surface with an angle of incidence of 30°. Calculate the angle between the ray and the normal after it leaves the water. (3)
(c) Another ray meets the surface with an angle of incidence of 60°. State and explain what happens to it. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) sin c = 1 ÷ n = 1 ÷ 1.33 1

sin c = 0.752 1

c = sin⁻¹ 0.752 = 49° 1

(b) n = sin i ÷ sin r, with the angle in air as i and 30° in water as r: 1.33 = sin i ÷ sin 30° 1

sin i = 1.33 × 0.5 = 0.665 1

Angle in air = sin⁻¹ 0.665 = 42° 1

(c) It is totally internally reflected back into the water 1

Because 60° is greater than the critical angle of 49°, and the light is going from water to air 1

In (b) the light is leaving the water, so the bigger angle is in the air. If you got 22°, you used the formula the wrong way round: the ray must bend away from the normal as it comes out.

(b) n = sin i ÷ sin r, with the angle in air as i and 30° in water as r: 1.33 = sin i ÷ sin 30°
Angle in air = sin⁻¹ 0.665 = 42°
(c) It is totally internally reflected back into the water

modules.title: Stars and the Universe
modules.standfirst: How a star's colour tells you its temperature, how stars are born and die, and how red-shift and the cosmic microwave background show the universe began with a Big Bang. This is a Year 11 topic (taught in Year 11, for the GCSE in summer 2027). Absolute magnitude, the HR diagram and all of cosmology (8.11P – 8.18P) are Physics-only.

intel.html:
This topic was in seven of the ten real Edexcel papers. Two kinds of question keep coming back. On stars, it is a "discuss the evolution" question worth 4 to 6 marks. On the universe, it is a red-shift calculation followed by "explain how this supports the Big Bang theory".

PaperWhat was asked
2024 Edexcel 1P Q4 (9)Evolution of a star: which energy stores rise or fall as a nebula collapses, the property that decides red giant or red supergiant (mass), then the differences between a red giant and a white dwarf
2024 Edexcel 2P Q1 (5)HR diagram with absolute magnitude against colour: match three regions to the objects in them, then define absolute magnitude
2023 Edexcel 2P Q7(b) (6)Two galaxies, reference wavelength 630 nm, observed 645 nm: the change in wavelength, the speed of the galaxy, then why "twice the red-shift, twice as far away" supports the Big Bang
2023 Edexcel 2P Q5(d)(i) (1)Multiple choice: the nuclear process that is the main energy source for stars (fusion)
2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q8 (8)Table of four stars with colour and mass: which is hottest, then discuss the evolution of Rigel (21 solar masses) and Sirius (2 solar masses)
2023 Edexcel Jan 2P Q8(b) (3)Light from a distant galaxy arrives with a longer wavelength: explain why this is evidence for the Big Bang
2022 Edexcel 2P Q6 (8)How the size and temperature of the universe have changed since the Big Bang, then discuss two pieces of evidence (6 marks)
2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q8 (7)Red-shift calculation (galaxy at 3.9 × 10⁴ km/s, wavelength 6.2 × 10⁻⁷ m), the received wavelength, then how red-shift supports the Big Bang

Fusion in the core of stars (2022 Jan 2P Q3) is taught in Module 6. The part you need here is simple: fusion is the energy source for stars.

On the 2023 red-shift calculation, the mark scheme punished one slip hard. Using the wavelength that arrived at Earth instead of the reference wavelength: "use of observed wavelength instead of 630 nm" … "gives 1 mark max".

λ₀ is always the reference wavelength: the one the light had when it was emitted, or measured in a lab. Never the observed one.

subsections.html: Module 9 covered the scale of things (billions of stars in a galaxy, billions of galaxies in the universe) and the basic Doppler effect. This module does two jobs. First, the life story of a star, which is decided almost entirely by its mass. Second, the life story of the universe, which is read from the light that reaches us.

subsections.heading: Colour tells you surface temperature
subsections.html:
Spec 8.7, 8.8 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q8(a)

A star's colour depends on its surface temperature: blue stars are the hottest and red stars are the coolest.

Think of heating a metal poker. First it glows dull red, then orange, then yellow-white. The hotter it gets, the more of its light is at the blue end of the spectrum. Stars work the same way. So astronomers can classify stars by colour, and the colour sorts them by temperature.

  1. Red: coolest surface (Betelgeuse)
  2. Orange
  3. Yellow: the Sun
  4. White and blue-white (Sirius)
  5. Blue: hottest surface (Rigel)

2023 Jan gave a table with each star's colour and its mass, then asked which star has the highest surface temperature. The mark scheme said "ignore links between mass and temperature".

✗ "Rigel, because it has the biggest mass."
✓ "Rigel, because it is blue, and a star's colour depends on its surface temperature."

subsections.heading: Birth: from nebula to main sequence star
subsections.html:
Spec 8.9, 7.25 · 2024 Edexcel 1P Q4(a) · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q8(b)

A star forms when a cloud of gas and dust, a nebula, collapses under gravity and gets hot enough for fusion to start.

  1. A nebula is a huge cloud of gas (mostly hydrogen) and dust.
  2. Gravity pulls part of it together, so it collapses.
  3. As it collapses, gravitational potential energy is transferred to the thermal store. The centre gets hotter and denser. This hot ball is a protostar.
  4. When the core is hot enough, nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium begins. The star is now a main sequence star.

2024 asked which energy stores change during the collapse, before the star forms. Work it out: the gas falls inwards, so its gravitational potential store decreases; it heats up, so its thermal store increases. Fusion has not started yet and nothing reacts chemically, so the nuclear and chemical stores stay the same.

"Protostar" is not one of the four stages the spec lists, but the 2023 mark scheme gave a mark for it. Use it.

subsections.heading: The main sequence: the long, stable part
subsections.html:
Spec 8.9, 7.25 · 2023 Edexcel 2P Q5(d)(i)

A main sequence star releases energy by fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, and it stays stable for most of its life.

Fusion is the energy source for stars (spec 7.25). Not fission, not burning. 2023 offered alpha decay, fission, fusion and gamma decay, and only fusion scored.

Why is it stable? Two effects are balanced. Gravity pulls the star inwards. The energy from fusion heats the core and makes an outward pressure. While the two balance, the star stays the same size. The Sun has been like this for about 4.6 billion years.

The main sequence ends when the hydrogen in the core runs out. What happens next depends on the star's mass.

subsections.heading: A star like the Sun: red giant, then white dwarf
subsections.html:
Spec 8.9 · 2024 Edexcel 1P Q4(b), (c) · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q8(b)

A star of similar mass to the Sun goes: nebula → main sequence star → red giant → white dwarf.

  1. The hydrogen in the core runs out.
  2. The star expands enormously. Its surface cools, so it glows red. It is now a red giant.
  3. Later the red giant throws off its outer layers as a glowing shell of gas, called a planetary nebula (nothing to do with planets).
  4. The core left behind is a white dwarf: very small, very hot and very dense. No fusion happens in it, so it slowly cools and fades.

Mark script: "discuss the evolution of a star like the Sun"

Began as a nebula (a cloud of gas and dust) · collapsed under gravity to form a protostar · fusion started, making a main sequence star · hydrogen in the core ran out, so it expanded into a red giant · lost its outer layers (planetary nebula), leaving a white dwarf.

2024 asked for the property that decides whether a star becomes a red giant or a red supergiant. The answer was mass, and the scheme said "ignore size, weight".

✗ "Its size." ✗ "Its weight."
✓ "Its mass."

subsections.heading: Red giant or white dwarf: the differences
subsections.html:
Spec 8.9 · 2024 Edexcel 1P Q4(c)

A red giant is huge, cool on the surface, very bright and still has fusion; a white dwarf is tiny, hot, dense, dim and has no fusion.

Red giantWhite dwarf
SizeEnormousTiny (about the size of the Earth)
Surface temperatureLower (red)Higher (white)
BrightnessMuch brighterDim
DensityLowVery high
FusionStill happeningNone
Planetary nebulaNoSurrounded by one

"Discuss the differences" wants comparisons. Each mark point names both stars: "the red giant is larger than the white dwarf". Four comparisons, four marks.

✗ "A red giant is big." That only describes one star.
✓ "A red giant is larger than a white dwarf, and has a lower surface temperature."

subsections.heading: Stars more massive than the Sun
subsections.html:
Spec 8.10 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q8(b) · 2024 Edexcel 1P Q4(b)

A star much more massive than the Sun goes: nebula → main sequence star → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole.

  1. Same start: nebula, protostar, main sequence. A massive main sequence star is hotter and bluer, and uses its hydrogen faster.
  2. When the hydrogen in the core runs out, it swells into a red supergiant.
  3. It then collapses and explodes as a supernova, which for a short time can outshine a whole galaxy.
  4. What is left depends on the mass: a neutron star (extremely dense), or, for the most massive stars, a black hole (gravity so strong that not even light can escape).

Mark script: 2023 Jan, Rigel (21 solar masses) and Sirius (2 solar masses)

Both: began in a nebula · were protostars · are main sequence stars.

Rigel: a high-mass star · becomes a red supergiant · then a supernova · then a neutron star (black hole was condoned).

Sirius: a low-mass star, similar to the Sun · becomes a red giant · eventually a white dwarf.

Six of these ten scored 6 marks. Notice the three "both" marks: say what the stars have in common before you split them.

subsections.heading: Absolute magnitude: brightness at a standard distance
subsections.html:
Spec 8.11P (Physics-only) · 2024 Edexcel 2P Q1(b)

Absolute magnitude is a measure of how bright a star would be if it were at a standard distance from us.

How bright a star looks depends on two things: how much light it gives out, and how far away it is. A dim star nearby can look brighter than a powerful star far away. To compare the stars themselves, imagine moving them all to the same distance. Their brightness at that distance is the absolute magnitude.

The scale runs backwards: the lower (more negative) the number, the brighter the star. A star of absolute magnitude −5 is far brighter than one of +10.

The 2024 definition was worth 2 marks: brightness (1) at a standard distance (1). "Fixed", "same" and "set" distance were all fine. The standard distance is 10 parsecs (about 32.6 light years), and the scheme said "ignore incorrect distance", so you do not need the number.

✗ "How bright a star is." Not enough: that is only 1 mark.
✓ "The brightness of a star at a standard distance."

subsections.heading: The Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram
subsections.html:
Spec 8.12P (Physics-only) · 2024 Edexcel 2P Q1(a)

The HR diagram plots absolute magnitude (brightness) against colour or surface temperature, and stars fall into clear groups on it.

How to draw it

Vertical axis: absolute magnitude. Brighter stars at the top (so the numbers get more negative as you go up).

Horizontal axis: colour or surface temperature. Hot blue stars on the left, cool red stars on the right. Temperature decreases from left to right.

Main sequence: a band from top left (hot, bright) to bottom right (cool, dim). The Sun sits in the middle of it.

Red giants and red supergiants: top right. Cool but very bright, because they are huge. Supergiants are highest.

White dwarfs: bottom left. Hot but dim, because they are tiny.

In 2024 the diagram had three labelled regions to match to objects. The list also included black hole, nebula, neutron star and supernova. None of those sit on an HR diagram as a region. The three regions are main sequence, red giants and white dwarfs.

The temperature axis runs the "wrong" way: hot on the left. ✗ Putting blue stars on the right. ✓ Blue and hot on the left, red and cool on the right.

And the scheme "reject mark if more than one line drawn from region". One line per region.

subsections.heading: The Big Bang: how the universe began and changed
subsections.html:
Spec 8.13P (Physics-only) · 2022 Edexcel 2P Q6(a)

The Big Bang theory says the universe began from a single point that was extremely small, hot and dense, and it has been expanding and cooling ever since.

  1. About 13.8 billion years ago, everything in the universe was in one tiny, extremely hot, dense point.
  2. It began to expand. As it expanded, it cooled.
  3. Over time, matter clumped under gravity to form stars and galaxies.
  4. It is still expanding today.

2022 asked how the size and temperature have changed. Two marks, one word each: expanding (getting larger) and cooling.

There are two main pieces of evidence: red-shift of galaxies and the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation. The rest of this section is about them.

subsections.heading: Red-shift: the Doppler effect for light
subsections.html:
Spec 8.15P (Physics-only) · 2023 Edexcel Jan 2P Q8(b)

When a light source moves away from us, the light we receive has a longer wavelength and a lower frequency: it is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum.

This is the Doppler effect from Module 9, applied to light.

  1. The galaxy moves away between sending out one wave crest and the next.
  2. So the crests arrive further apart: the observed wavelength increases.
  3. The speed of light does not change, so by v = f × λ the observed frequency decreases.
  4. Longer wavelength means the light is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum: red-shift.

A source moving towards us gives the opposite: shorter wavelength, higher frequency, a blue-shift.

How do astronomers know the wavelength changed? Elements such as hydrogen absorb or emit light at exact wavelengths. They know those wavelengths from the lab. That is the reference wavelength, λ₀. In light from a galaxy, the same pattern appears, but moved to longer wavelengths.

✗ "The light turns red." It doesn't. It is shifted towards the red end: every wavelength gets longer.
✗ "The light slows down." The speed of light is constant; the wavelength and frequency change.

subsections.heading: The red-shift equation
subsections.html:
Spec 8.16P (Physics-only) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q8(a) · 2023 Edexcel 2P Q7(b)(i), (ii)

The fractional change in wavelength equals the galaxy's speed divided by the speed of light.

Δλ ÷ λ₀ = v ÷ c (on the formula sheet)
Δλ = change in wavelength (observed − reference) · λ₀ = reference wavelength · v = velocity of the galaxy · c = speed of light = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s

Δλ and λ₀ just need the same unit as each other (both nm, or both m). v and c need the same unit as each other too (both m/s, or both km/s). You do not need to convert nm to m, because the units cancel in the ratio.

Worked: 2023 Edexcel 2P Q7(b)

Reference wavelength 630 nm, observed 645 nm.

(i) Δλ = 645 − 630 = 15 nm

(ii) 15 ÷ 630 = v ÷ (3.0 × 10⁸) → v = (15 ÷ 630) × 3.0 × 10⁸ = 7.1 × 10⁶ m/s

Worked: 2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q8(a)

Galaxy moves away at 3.9 × 10⁴ km/s; c = 3.0 × 10⁵ km/s; emitted wavelength 6.2 × 10⁻⁷ m.

(i) Δλ = 6.2 × 10⁻⁷ × (3.9 × 10⁴ ÷ 3.0 × 10⁵) = 8.1 × 10⁻⁸ m

(ii) Received wavelength = 6.2 × 10⁻⁷ + 8.1 × 10⁻⁸ = 7.0 × 10⁻⁷ m. It is longer, because the galaxy is moving away.

✗ Dividing by the observed wavelength (645 nm). That gave 7.0 × 10⁶ m/s and 1 mark at most.
✓ Divide by the reference wavelength, λ₀ = 630 nm.

✗ Giving Δλ as the answer to "calculate the wavelength received". ✓ Add Δλ back on to λ₀.

subsections.heading: Red-shift and distance: why the universe is expanding
subsections.html:
Spec 8.17P, 8.18P (Physics-only) · 2022 Edexcel Jan 2P Q8(b) · 2023 Edexcel 2P Q7(b)(iii) · 2023 Edexcel Jan 2P Q8(b) · 2022 Edexcel 2P Q6(b)

Light from almost all distant galaxies is red-shifted, and the further away a galaxy is, the greater its red-shift, so the further away, the faster it is moving away: the universe is expanding.

  1. Light from distant galaxies is red-shifted, so they are moving away from us.
  2. The further away the galaxy, the greater the red-shift.
  3. A greater red-shift means the galaxy is moving away faster.
  4. So the further away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away. Speed is directly proportional to distance.
  5. This means the galaxies are all moving apart: the universe is expanding.
  6. Run the expansion backwards and everything was once at a single point. That is the Big Bang.

Mark script: 2023 2P Q7(b)(iii), two marks

"Galaxy B has twice the red-shift of galaxy A and is twice as far away."

Twice the red-shift means twice the speed (1) · so the further away a galaxy is, the faster it moves away, meaning galaxies are moving apart (1).

The scheme said to "ignore references to single point/singularity, universe expansion, Big Bang itself" here. On this part, the marks were only for linking red-shift, speed and distance.

The 2022 scheme accepted "star" for "galaxy", but don't rely on it. Say galaxy.

✗ "The galaxies are red-shifted, so the Big Bang happened." That skips the steps that carry the marks.
✓ "The further away the galaxy, the greater the red-shift, so the faster it is moving away. So the universe is expanding, and must have started from a single point."

subsections.heading: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation
subsections.html:
Spec 8.14P (Physics-only) · 2022 Edexcel 2P Q6(b)

The CMB is microwave radiation that reaches us from every direction in space; it is left over from the hot early universe, stretched to longer wavelengths as the universe expanded.

  1. Just after the Big Bang the universe was extremely hot and gave out high-energy, short-wavelength radiation.
  2. As the universe expanded, that radiation was stretched: its wavelength increased.
  3. Today it has reached the microwave part of the spectrum.
  4. It is almost the same in all directions. That suggests all parts of the universe were once in contact, at a single hot point.

Mark script: 2022 2P Q6(b), "discuss two pieces of evidence" (6 marks)

Up to four marks on each piece of evidence.

CMB: name the cosmic microwave background radiation · it is the same in all directions / everywhere · so all parts of the universe were in contact long ago · its wavelength has increased as the universe expanded · the universe was much hotter long ago.

Red-shift: name the red-shift of galaxies · the further away the galaxy, the greater the red-shift · greater red-shift means faster · so the further away, the faster it moves away · galaxies moving apart means expansion from a single point.

Write at least three points on each. A six-mark answer on only one piece of evidence can score at most four.

2023 Jan asked why a red-shifted galaxy is evidence for the Big Bang, and the scheme said "ignore CMBR". Answer the evidence you were given.

The sentences behind most of the marks

Colour: a star's colour depends on its surface temperature. Blue is hottest, red is coolest.

Sun-like star: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → white dwarf (with a planetary nebula).

Massive star: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole.

What decides the path: the star's mass.

Energy source: fusion of hydrogen into helium.

Absolute magnitude: brightness at a standard distance. Lower number = brighter.

HR diagram: absolute magnitude up the side, colour/temperature along the bottom with hot on the left. Main sequence diagonal; giants top right; white dwarfs bottom left.

Red-shift: further galaxy → greater red-shift → faster moving away → universe expanding → began at a single point.

CMB: microwave radiation from all directions, left over from the hot early universe, stretched by the expansion.

questions.promptHtml: Betelgeuse is red and Rigel is blue. Both are in the constellation Orion. Which has the hotter surface, and why can you tell just by looking?
questions.answerHtml:
Rigel. A star's colour depends on its surface temperature.

Anything hot glows. As it gets hotter, more of its light is at shorter wavelengths, towards the blue end. A cooler surface gives off more red light. So a blue star has a hotter surface than a red one.

That is why colour can be used to classify stars: it sorts them by surface temperature without anyone needing to visit them.

questions.promptHtml: A main sequence star stays the same size for billions of years, even though gravity is pulling all its gas inwards. Why doesn't it collapse?
questions.answerHtml:
Fusion in the core releases a huge amount of energy. That keeps the core very hot and produces an outward pressure.

Gravity pulls inwards. While the outward pressure balances gravity, the star stays stable.

When the hydrogen in the core runs out, the balance changes, and the star leaves the main sequence. That is why "the hydrogen runs out" is the trigger for the red giant or red supergiant stage.

questions.promptHtml: Two stars form in the same nebula at the same time. One has the mass of the Sun, the other has 20 times as much. Explain why they end up so differently.
questions.answerHtml:
Their early lives are the same: nebula, protostar, main sequence. The difference is mass.

The Sun-like star becomes a red giant, sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula, and leaves a white dwarf.

The massive star becomes a red supergiant, explodes as a supernova, and leaves a neutron star or, if it is massive enough, a black hole.

This is why 2024 asked for "the property that determines" the path: the one-word answer is mass. Size and weight were ignored.

questions.promptHtml: On the HR diagram, white dwarfs are hotter than the Sun but much dimmer. Red giants are cooler than the Sun but much brighter. How can both be true?
questions.answerHtml:
How bright a star is depends on its temperature and on its size.

A white dwarf is very hot, so each bit of its surface is bright. But it is tiny, about the size of the Earth, so there is very little surface. Total: dim. That puts it bottom left.

A red giant is cooler, so each bit of surface gives out less. But it is enormous, so it has a vast surface. Total: very bright. That puts it top right.

So on the HR diagram, stars above the main sequence are bigger than main sequence stars of the same colour, and stars below it are smaller.

questions.promptHtml: Why do astronomers bother with absolute magnitude? Why not just measure how bright each star looks?
questions.answerHtml:
How bright a star looks from Earth depends on how far away it is, not just on how much light it gives out. A modest star close by can look brighter than a giant far away.

Absolute magnitude removes the distance problem. It is the brightness the star would have at a standard distance. Now every star is compared fairly, like measuring everyone's height standing on the same floor.

That is why the HR diagram uses absolute magnitude. Using how bright stars look would scatter them randomly, and the main sequence would vanish.

questions.promptHtml: Almost every galaxy is moving away from us. Does that mean the Earth is at the centre of the universe?
questions.answerHtml:
No. Think of a loaf of raisin bread rising in the oven. Every raisin moves away from every other raisin. A raisin twice as far away moves away twice as fast, because there is twice as much dough between them expanding.

From any raisin, all the others seem to rush away. There is nothing special about the one you are on.

It is the same with galaxies. From any galaxy, the others seem to move away, faster the further away they are. That pattern (speed proportional to distance) is exactly what you expect if the whole universe is expanding. That is why it supports the Big Bang.

questions.promptHtml: The early universe was extremely hot, so the radiation it gave out had very short wavelengths. So why is the leftover radiation now in the microwave region?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the universe has been expanding ever since, and the radiation has been stretched with it.

As space expands, the wavelength of the radiation travelling through it increases. Over billions of years it has been stretched from very short wavelengths all the way to microwaves.

So the CMB is evidence for two things at once: that the universe was once very hot, and that it has expanded. The 2022 scheme gave marks for both ideas.

questions.promptHtml: In Δλ ÷ λ₀ = v ÷ c, why must λ₀ be the reference wavelength and not the observed one? And why can you leave both wavelengths in nanometres?
questions.answerHtml:
λ₀ is the wavelength the light had when it was emitted. The equation compares the change with that starting value. The observed wavelength already contains the change, so dividing by it gives the wrong fraction. In 2023 that cost all but 1 mark.

The left side is a ratio of two wavelengths. If both are in nm, the nm cancel, and you get a plain number. The same goes for v ÷ c: if c is in km/s, v comes out in km/s.

Example: a hydrogen line with λ₀ = 656 nm is observed at 663 nm. Δλ = 7 nm, so v = (7 ÷ 656) × 3.0 × 10⁸ ≈ 3.2 × 10⁶ m/s, moving away.

modules.title: Thermal Energy Transfer
modules.standfirst: How energy gets from hot things to cold things: by conduction, convection and radiation, and how we slow it down. The physics is simple; the marks go to people who name the mechanism and explain it with particles, density or infrared. This is a Year 11 topic, taught in Year 11 for the GCSE in summer 2027.

intel.html:
This topic turned up in six of the ten real Edexcel papers from 2022 to 2024, for about 29 marks in total. It is never a calculation. It is always explain: why snow melts slowly, why a black bar heats up faster, why a lid changes a result, or a 6-mark method for the infrared practical.

2024 Edexcel 1P Q3(d) (2)Infrared heating lamps: explain why white paint takes longer to harden than black paint
2024 Edexcel 2P Q3 (8)Practical: describe a method to compare the infrared absorbed by a black bottle and a silver bottle (6 marks), then sketch both temperature–time curves

Two patterns. Surfaces and infrared come up almost every year: black absorbs and emits well, white and shiny do not. And the examiners want the mechanism named: conduction through the metal, convection in the water or air, radiation as infrared.

On the snow question, the mark for energy flow from the drain cover to the snow came with this note: "must be correct direction of energy transfer". Energy goes from the warmer metal into the colder snow. "The cold goes into the metal" scores nothing.

On the black and silver bottles graph: "reject whole response if both lines show a decrease". The bottles are being heated, so both lines rise, and the black one is always above.

And from the school's marking of the hot-water-in-a-cup question: "“Heat rises” scores nothing — name the transfer mechanism."

subsections.html: Three mechanisms, one rule. Energy is transferred from hotter places to colder places, and it does it by conduction, convection or radiation. Every question in this topic is asking you which one, and why. This module builds on the cooling-curve work in Module 2 (Solids, Liquids and Gases) and the energy stores in Module 8 (Energy).

subsections.heading: The one rule: hot to cold
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q10(b)

Thermal energy is always transferred from a hotter object to a colder one, and it keeps going until they reach the same temperature. The bigger the temperature difference, the faster the transfer.

When the two temperatures are equal the objects are in thermal equilibrium and there is no more net transfer. That is why a cooling curve levels off: as the temperature difference shrinks, the rate of transfer shrinks with it.

MechanismNeeds particles?Main place it happens
ConductionYesSolids, especially metals
ConvectionYes, and they must be free to moveLiquids and gases (fluids)
RadiationNoAnywhere, including a vacuum

✗ "The cold spreads into the drink."

✓ "Energy is transferred from the warmer drink to the colder ice."

Cold is not a thing that moves. Only energy moves, and only from hot to cold. The 2023 snow scheme insisted on the correct direction of energy transfer.

subsections.heading: Conduction: particles passing on vibrations
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6 · 2023 Edexcel 1P Q8(b) · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q10(b)

In conduction, energy passes through a material from particle to particle, without the material itself moving.

Heat one end of a solid rod and this happens:

  1. The particles at the hot end gain energy and vibrate more.
  2. They are closely packed, so they bump into their neighbours and pass on some of that energy.
  3. Those neighbours vibrate more and pass energy on in turn.
  4. Energy spreads along the rod from the hot end to the cold end.

Conduction is best in solids, where particles are packed closely together. It is poor in liquids and very poor in gases, where the particles are further apart.

subsections.heading: Why metals are the best conductors
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6 · 2023 Edexcel 1P Q8(b)

Metals conduct well because they contain free electrons, which move through the metal and carry energy quickly from the hot part to the cold part.

Every solid conducts by vibrating particles. Metals have this and a sea of free (delocalised) electrons. These electrons gain energy at the hot end, travel through the metal and give energy to particles further along. That is much faster than vibrations alone.

Materials that conduct poorly are insulators: wood, plastic, glass, wool, and above all air. That is why a pan has a plastic handle and why so much insulation works by trapping air.

The drain-cover mark script (2023 Edexcel 1P Q8(b))

Snow melts faster on a metal drain cover than on the ground. The two marks were for any two of:

the drain cover is warmer than the snow · metal is a good conductor · energy is transferred from the drain cover to the snow.

subsections.heading: Convection: warm fluid rises, cool fluid sinks
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6 · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q10(b)

In convection, energy is carried by the fluid itself moving: warmer fluid is less dense and rises, and cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place.

A fluid is a liquid or a gas. Its particles can move from place to place, so the hot part can travel. The chain is always the same:

  1. The fluid near the heat source gains energy. Its particles move faster and spread further apart.
  2. So that part of the fluid expands and becomes less dense.
  3. The less dense fluid rises.
  4. Cooler, denser fluid sinks to replace it, and is then heated in turn.
  5. This circulation is a convection current.

Convection cannot happen in a solid, because its particles are fixed in place. It cannot happen in a vacuum, because there is nothing to move.

✗ "Heat rises."

✓ "The warmer air rises because it is less dense."

✗ "The particles expand."

✓ "The particles move further apart, so the air expands."

Particles do not get bigger when they are heated. The fluid expands because the gaps between the particles grow.

subsections.heading: Convection in everyday life
subsections.html:
Spec 4.7 · 2023 Edexcel 1P Q8(c)

Heat from below and convection spreads it upwards; cool from above and convection spreads it downwards. That idea explains where heaters, kettle elements and freezer compartments are put.

SituationWhat convection does
Room heater (often called a radiator)Air next to it warms, becomes less dense and rises. Cooler air sinks and flows across the floor towards the heater. A convection current heats the whole room. Most of its energy is transferred by convection, despite the name.
Kettle element at the bottomWater at the bottom warms and rises. Cooler water sinks to the element, so all the water gets heated.
Freezer compartment at the top of a fridgeAir cooled at the top becomes denser and sinks. Warmer air rises to be cooled. The whole fridge is cooled.
Sea breeze on a sunny dayThe land warms faster than the sea. Air above the land warms and rises; cooler air from over the sea moves in to replace it.
Snow on a still dayWarmer air rises away from the snow. The coldest, densest air stays next to the snow, so less energy is transferred to it and it melts more slowly.

The snow mark script (2023 Edexcel 1P Q8(c))

"Explain how a convection current above the snow increases the time taken for the snow to melt." Two marks from:

warmer air rises · colder air is nearest the snow · the rate of energy transfer from the air to the snow decreases.

The scheme said to ignore "nearest the ground". It is the snow the cold air sits on that matters.

subsections.heading: Radiation: infrared needs no medium
subsections.html:
Spec 4.6 · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1P Q8(d) · 2024 Edexcel 1P Q3

Thermal radiation is energy carried by infrared waves, which are electromagnetic waves, so it needs no particles and can travel through a vacuum.

This makes radiation different from the other two. Conduction and convection both need particles. Radiation does not. It is the only way energy can cross empty space, which is how energy from the Sun reaches the Earth.

All objects emit infrared radiation, all the time. They also absorb it. An object that emits more than it absorbs cools down. An object that absorbs more than it emits warms up.

2022's satellite question gave a mark for saying that conduction and convection play no part outside the spacecraft, and another for the reason: there are no particles in space. Say both halves.

✗ "Radiation needs air to travel through."

✓ "Infrared is an electromagnetic wave, so it can travel through a vacuum."

subsections.heading: Surfaces: absorbers and reflectors
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8 · 2023 Edexcel 1P Q8(a) · 2024 Edexcel 1P Q3(d)

Dark, matt surfaces are good absorbers of infrared radiation; light, shiny surfaces are poor absorbers and good reflectors.

SurfaceAbsorbing infraredEmitting infrared
Dark and matt (dull black)Best absorberBest emitter
Light and shiny (white, silver)Poor absorber, good reflectorPoor emitter

So in the same sunshine, a black car roof gets hotter than a white one. White snow reflects most of the Sun's infrared, so it absorbs little energy and melts slowly even in direct sunlight.

The two-mark pattern (2023 Edexcel 1P Q8(a), 2024 Edexcel 1P Q3(d))

Mark 1: name the process, absorption or reflection of infrared.

Mark 2: link it to the colour, e.g. white is a poor absorber / good reflector, or black is a better absorber, so more energy is transferred to it in the same time.

2024's scheme noted that "black car absorbs more energy/heat" alone scores both marks. The words absorbs and more energy do the work.

subsections.heading: Emission depends on surface and temperature
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8 · 2022 Edexcel Jan 1P Q8(d)

The hotter an object is, the more infrared radiation it emits; and at the same temperature, a dark matt surface emits more than a light shiny one.

A good absorber is also a good emitter. That is why a black object heats up fastest in the Sun and cools down fastest in the shade.

The spinning satellite (2022 Edexcel Jan 1P Q8(d), 4 marks)

A dull black bar and a shiny white bar turn towards and away from the Sun. The marks were for any four of:

  1. Both bars warm up facing the Sun and cool down facing away.
  2. Facing the Sun, the black bar's temperature rises faster, because black is a better absorber of radiation.
  3. So the black bar reaches a higher temperature.
  4. Facing away, the black bar's temperature falls faster, because black is a better emitter of radiation.
  5. Conduction and convection play no part outside the spacecraft, because there are no particles in space.

subsections.heading: Practical: infrared absorbed by different surfaces
subsections.html:
Spec 4.9 · 2024 Edexcel 2P Q3 — 8 marks, 6 of them for the method

Heat two identical containers of water, one black and one silver, with the same infrared heater, and compare how fast the water temperature rises. The water that warms faster is in the better absorber.

  1. Put an equal volume of water in the black bottle and the silver bottle.
  2. Check the water in both starts at the same temperature.
  3. Place both bottles the same distance from the heater, with the same heater setting for both.
  4. Switch on and measure the temperature of both after a set time (or every minute).
  5. Repeat the whole investigation and calculate a mean.
  6. Safety: do not touch the hot heater (burns) and keep water away from the mains (electrocution).

The result: the black bottle's water warms faster. On a temperature–time graph both lines rise and the black line is always above the silver line.

2024's graph mark: "reject whole response if both lines show a decrease". The bottles are being heated. If you draw cooling curves, you get nothing for that part.

The same apparatus run the other way round, with hot water left to cool, tests emission: the water in the black bottle cools faster. Read which one the question describes.

subsections.heading: Practicals: conduction and convection
subsections.html:
Spec 4.9

For conduction, compare how quickly energy travels along rods of different materials; for convection, make the moving water visible with a coloured crystal.

Conduction. Take rods of different metals of the same length and thickness. Stick a drawing pin to the far end of each with a small blob of wax (or petroleum jelly). Heat the other ends equally, for example by standing them in the same hot water. Time how long each pin takes to fall. The shortest time means the best conductor.

Convection. Drop a small crystal of potassium manganate(VII) (potassium permanganate) at the bottom of a beaker of water, at one side. Heat gently under the crystal. The purple colour rises above the heat, spreads across the top and sinks on the far side: you can see the convection current.

Radiation (emission). A metal cube with faces of different surfaces (matt black, white, shiny silver) is filled with hot water. An infrared detector is held the same distance from each face in turn. The matt black face gives the highest reading and the shiny silver face the lowest.

subsections.heading: Reducing unwanted transfer: insulating a house
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10

Most insulation works by trapping air: air is a poor conductor, and when it is trapped in small pockets it cannot form convection currents.

MethodHow it worksTransfer reduced
Loft insulation (fibreglass or mineral wool)Traps air between the fibresConduction and convection through the roof
Cavity wall insulation (foam or fibre)Fills the gap between the two walls and traps air in small pockets, so no convection currents form in the cavityConvection (and conduction) across the cavity
Double glazingA layer of air (or a vacuum) between two panes of glassConduction (and convection)
Draught excludersBlock gaps round doors and windowsConvection: warm air escaping
Shiny foil behind a radiatorReflects infrared back into the roomRadiation into the wall

The same trapped-air idea explains why wool jumpers, duvets, feathers and fur keep things warm.

✗ "Air is a good insulator, so the cavity can be left empty."

✓ An empty cavity lets the air circulate in convection currents. Foam traps the air so it cannot move. Air is only a good insulator when it is trapped.

subsections.heading: The vacuum flask
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10

A vacuum flask reduces all three kinds of transfer: the vacuum stops conduction and convection, and the silvered surfaces reduce radiation.

FeatureTransfer it reducesWhy
Vacuum between two glass wallsConduction and convectionBoth need particles, and a vacuum has none
Silvered (shiny) wallsRadiationShiny surfaces are poor emitters and reflect infrared back
Stopper (plastic or cork)Convection and evaporation from the top; conductionStops warm air or vapour escaping, and is a poor conductor
Insulated supports and outer caseConductionPoor conductors hold the inner bottle

It works in both directions. It keeps hot drinks hot and cold drinks cold, because it slows energy transfer whichever way it is going.

✗ "The vacuum stops radiation."

✓ Radiation can cross a vacuum. The vacuum stops conduction and convection; the silvering reduces radiation.

subsections.heading: Lids and insulation in experiments
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10 · 2022 Edexcel 2P Q7(b) · 2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q10(c)

In any heating experiment, energy lost to the surroundings makes the result less accurate, so insulate the container and put a lid on it.

An open cup of hot water loses energy from its surface by convection and evaporation, and from its sides by conduction and radiation. A lid cuts the losses from the top; lagging or a polystyrene cup cuts them from the sides.

The lid mark script (2023 Edexcel Jan 1P Q10(c), 3 marks)

Putting a lid on the cup:

  1. reduces the energy transfer by convection and radiation (evaporation also accepted);
  2. so the equilibrium temperature is higher;
  3. and it takes longer to cool to room temperature.

2022's improvement question (Q7(b)) accepted adding insulation, a lid, or a container with low thermal conductivity, such as a polystyrene cup.

The sentences behind most of the marks

Direction: energy is transferred from the hotter object to the colder one until they reach the same temperature.

Conduction: particles vibrate more and pass energy to neighbouring particles. Metals are best because of free electrons.

Convection: warmer fluid is less dense and rises; cooler, denser fluid sinks; this sets up a convection current. Only in liquids and gases.

Radiation: infrared electromagnetic waves. Needs no medium, so it is the only way across a vacuum.

Surfaces: dark matt = best absorber and best emitter. Light shiny = poor absorber, poor emitter, good reflector.

Temperature: the hotter an object, the more infrared it emits.

Insulation: trapped air is a poor conductor and cannot form convection currents.

Vacuum flask: vacuum stops conduction and convection; silvering reduces radiation; stopper reduces convection and evaporation.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:

Thermal equilibriumWhen objects are at the same temperature, so there is no net energy transfer between them
