questions.promptHtml: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been in the same drawer all night, so they are at the same temperature. Why does the metal one feel colder when you pick it up?
questions.hint: What your hand actually senses: temperature, or energy leaving it?
questions.answerHtml:
Both spoons are colder than your hand, so energy is transferred from your hand to the spoon.

Metal is a good conductor, thanks to its free electrons. It carries energy away from your skin quickly, so your hand loses energy fast and feels cold.

Wood is an insulator. It takes energy from your skin slowly, so your hand barely cools.

The point: your skin senses the rate of energy transfer, not the object's temperature. Same temperature, different conductors, different feel.

questions.promptHtml: Why can convection happen in water and air but never in a solid block of iron?
questions.answerHtml:
Convection means the warm material itself moves: it rises because it is less dense, and cooler material sinks to replace it.

In a liquid or a gas the particles are free to move from place to place, so a whole region of warm fluid can flow upwards.

In a solid the particles are fixed in position. They can only vibrate. Nothing can flow, so energy can only pass through the iron by conduction.

questions.promptHtml: "Heat rises" sounds right. Why does it score nothing?
questions.answerHtml:
Because heat is energy, and energy does not rise. It goes from hot to cold in any direction: sideways along a rod, downwards into a cold floor.

What rises is warm fluid, and it rises for a reason: its particles have moved further apart, so it is less dense than the cooler fluid around it. The cooler, denser fluid sinks and pushes it up.

The fix: always say what rises (the warmer air or water) and why (less dense). The school's marking of this exact question said the mechanism must be named.

questions.promptHtml: A black car gets hotter than a white car in the sun. At night, the black car also cools down faster. How can the same colour make it both heat up and cool down faster?
questions.answerHtml:
A dark matt surface is a good absorber of infrared and a good emitter of infrared. The two go together.

In the sun, more infrared arrives than the car emits. The black car absorbs more of it, so it warms faster.

At night, there is little infrared arriving. The car is now emitting more than it absorbs, and the black car emits more, so it cools faster.

This is exactly the 2022 satellite question: the black bar warmed faster facing the Sun and cooled faster facing away.

questions.promptHtml: A vacuum flask is advertised for hot coffee. Will it keep an iced drink cold too? Explain.
questions.answerHtml:
Yes. A vacuum flask does not "keep heat in". It reduces energy transfer, in either direction.

With an iced drink, energy would flow in from the warmer room. The vacuum still blocks conduction and convection, because there are no particles to carry the energy. The silvered walls still reduce radiation, now by reflecting infrared from outside back out. The stopper still stops warm air getting in.

So the drink warms up very slowly. Whatever the direction, the same three features slow it down.

questions.promptHtml: Air can carry energy very well by convection: that is how a heater warms a room. So how can air also be the key ingredient in almost every insulator?
questions.answerHtml:
Air is a very poor conductor: its particles are far apart, so they rarely pass on vibrations. Its only way of carrying much energy is convection, which needs the air to move.

Insulators like wool, foam, fibreglass and feathers trap the air in tiny pockets. The air cannot flow, so no convection currents can form. Now it is left with conduction only, and it is bad at that.

That is why an empty wall cavity is poor (the air circulates) but a cavity filled with foam is good (the same air, trapped).

questions.promptHtml: On a still, clear day, why does a convection current in the air slow down the melting of snow? Surely moving air should warm it up?
questions.hint: Which air ends up touching the snow?
questions.answerHtml:
Air touching the snow is cooled by it. Cooler air is denser, so it stays low. Warmer air rises away.

So the convection current sorts the air: the coldest air sits nearest the snow. The temperature difference between the snow and the air touching it is small.

A small temperature difference means a slow rate of energy transfer to the snow, so it takes longer to melt. These were exactly the three marking points in 2023 Edexcel 1P Q8(c).

A wind would be different: it would keep bringing warmer air to the snow. Convection on a still day does the opposite.

questions.promptHtml: Energy reaches us from the Sun across 150 million km of space. Why can it only arrive by radiation, and not by conduction or convection?
questions.answerHtml:
Space is (almost) a vacuum: there are no particles in it.

Conduction needs particles to vibrate and pass energy on. Convection needs a fluid that can move. With no particles, neither can happen.

Radiation is carried by infrared (electromagnetic) waves, which need no medium at all. So it is the only way across.

2022's satellite question gave a mark for exactly this: convection and conduction play no part outside the spacecraft, because there are no particles there.

understanding.intro: These are not exam questions. They are the "why" questions that make the exam questions easy. Try each one properly before opening the answer.

questions.promptHtml:
Infrared heating lamps are used to harden fresh paint on cars. Paint hardens faster when it absorbs more energy.

(a) A technician notices that white paint takes longer to harden than black paint. Explain this observation. (2)
(b) Explain why energy from the Sun reaches the Earth by radiation, but not by conduction or convection. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Black is a better absorber of infrared radiation (or white is a better reflector) 1

So more energy is transferred to the black paint in the same time 1

(b) Space is a vacuum: there are no particles 1

Conduction and convection need particles, but infrared is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium 1

(a) is modelled on 2024 Edexcel 1P Q3(d), where "black absorbs more energy" alone earned both marks.

markScheme.point: (a) Black is a better absorber of infrared radiation (or white is a better reflector)
So more energy is transferred to the black paint in the same time
(b) Space is a vacuum: there are no particles
Conduction and convection need particles, but infrared is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium

questions.promptHtml:
One end of a copper rod is held in a flame. Soon the other end is hot.

(a) Explain how energy is transferred along the rod. (2)
(b) Explain why a copper rod gets hot at the far end much sooner than a glass rod of the same size. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Particles at the hot end gain energy and vibrate more 1

They pass energy on to neighbouring particles, so energy is conducted along the rod 1

(b) Copper is a metal and has free electrons 1

The free electrons move through the metal and carry energy quickly to the cold end; glass has none 1

markScheme.point: (a) Particles at the hot end gain energy and vibrate more

The free electrons move through the metal and carry energy quickly to the cold end; glass has none

questions.promptHtml:
An electric heater stands against the wall of a cold room. After a while the whole room is warm.

Explain how the heater warms the whole room. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Air next to the heater gains energy and warms up 1

The warm air expands and becomes less dense 1

So the warm air rises 1

Cooler, denser air sinks to take its place and is heated in turn, setting up a convection current 1

"Heat rises" would earn none of these. Every mark names what moves and why.

markScheme.point: Air next to the heater gains energy and warms up
The warm air expands and becomes less dense
So the warm air rises
Cooler, denser air sinks to take its place and is heated in turn, setting up a convection current

questions.promptHtml:
A vacuum flask has a double-walled glass bottle with a vacuum between the walls. The walls are silvered. The top is closed with a plastic stopper.

Explain how each of these features reduces the energy transferred from hot soup inside the flask. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
The vacuum prevents conduction across the gap 1

The vacuum prevents convection across the gap 1

because both need particles, and a vacuum has none 1

The silvered (shiny) surfaces reduce energy transfer by radiation, as they are poor emitters and reflect infrared back towards the soup 1

The stopper stops warm air and vapour escaping, reducing convection and evaporation from the top 1

The stopper is plastic, a poor conductor, so it reduces conduction through the top 1

The classic slip: saying the vacuum stops radiation. It does not. Radiation crosses a vacuum; that is how sunlight reaches us.

questions.promptHtml:
A homeowner fits loft insulation made of mineral wool, and has foam injected into the cavity between the house's inner and outer walls.

Explain how these reduce the energy transferred out of the house. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Both materials trap air in small pockets 1

Air is a poor conductor, so little energy is transferred by conduction 1

The trapped air cannot move, so convection currents cannot form 1

In the cavity, the foam stops the air circulating between the two walls, so energy is not carried across the cavity by convection 1

questions.promptHtml:
A student has rods of copper, iron and aluminium, some wax, some drawing pins, a beaker of very hot water and a stopwatch.

Describe how the student could use this equipment to find which metal is the best thermal conductor. (5)
questions.answerHtml:
Use rods of the same length and thickness 1

Fix a drawing pin to the top end of each rod with the same amount of wax 1

Stand the other ends of all three rods in the same hot water at the same time, to the same depth 1

Time how long it takes for each pin to fall off 1

The rod whose pin falls first (shortest time) is the best conductor 1

Also creditworthy: repeat and take a mean; take care with the hot water.

markScheme.point: Use rods of the same length and thickness
Fix a drawing pin to the top end of each rod with the same amount of wax
Stand the other ends of all three rods in the same hot water at the same time, to the same depth
Time how long it takes for each pin to fall off
The rod whose pin falls first (shortest time) is the best conductor

questions.promptHtml:
A student drops a small purple crystal of potassium manganate(VII) to the bottom of a beaker of cold water, at one side. He heats the beaker gently, directly under the crystal.

(a) Describe what the student would see. (2)
(b) Explain your answer to (a). (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) The purple colour rises above the crystal 1

It then moves across the top of the water and sinks down the other side, showing a circulating current 1

(b) Water above the flame is heated and becomes less dense 1

So it rises, carrying the dye with it 1

Cooler, denser water sinks to replace it, forming a convection current 1

questions.promptHtml:
(a) The freezer compartment in a fridge is at the top. Explain how this helps to cool all the food in the fridge. (3)
(b) The heating element in an electric kettle is at the bottom. Explain why. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Air near the freezer is cooled and becomes denser 1

So it sinks, while warmer air from lower down rises to be cooled 1

This sets up a convection current that circulates cold air round the whole fridge 1

(b) Water heated at the bottom becomes less dense and rises 1

Cooler, denser water sinks to the element to be heated, so convection heats all the water 1

So it sinks, while warmer air from lower down rises to be cooled
This sets up a convection current that circulates cold air round the whole fridge
(b) Water heated at the bottom becomes less dense and rises
Cooler, denser water sinks to the element to be heated, so convection heats all the water

questions.promptHtml:
A student finds the specific heat capacity of water. She heats an aluminium block in an oven, drops it into water in an open metal can, and records the highest temperature the water reaches.

(a) Give two ways she could improve her method to make her value more accurate. (2)
(b) Explain how a lid on the can would change the maximum temperature the water reaches. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Any two from: insulate the can (e.g. wrap it in wool); put a lid on it; use a container with low thermal conductivity, such as a polystyrene cup; move the block from oven to water as quickly as possible; repeat and take a mean.

Insulate the can 1

Use a lid 1

(b) The lid reduces energy lost from the water surface by convection and evaporation 1

So more of the energy stays in the water and the maximum temperature is higher (closer to the true value) 1

(a) is modelled on 2022 Edexcel 2P Q7(b).

markScheme.point: Insulate the can
Use a lid
(b) The lid reduces energy lost from the water surface by convection and evaporation

questions.promptHtml:
A saucepan of water is heated on an electric hot plate. The pan has a copper base, a plastic handle, a shiny outer surface and a lid.

Explain how energy is transferred to all of the water, and how the design of the pan affects energy transfer. Refer to conduction, convection and radiation in your answer. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Energy is conducted through the copper base: particles vibrate and pass on energy, and free electrons carry it quickly 1

Water at the bottom is heated, becomes less dense and rises 1

Cooler, denser water sinks to the base to be heated, so a convection current heats all the water 1

The plastic handle is a poor conductor, so little energy is conducted to the cook's hand 1

The shiny outer surface is a poor emitter, so less energy is lost by radiation 1

The lid reduces energy lost from the top by convection and evaporation 1

Six marks, six named mechanisms. Structure long answers like this one: one feature, one mechanism, one reason per line.

markScheme.point: Energy is conducted through the copper base: particles vibrate and pass on energy, and free electrons carry it quickly
Water at the bottom is heated, becomes less dense and rises
Cooler, denser water sinks to the base to be heated, so a convection current heats all the water
The plastic handle is a poor conductor, so little energy is conducted to the cook's hand
The shiny outer surface is a poor emitter, so less energy is lost by radiation
The lid reduces energy lost from the top by convection and evaporation
